articles.title_orig: Coco Gauff Says Racist Abuse Has Been ‘Draining’ at China Open
articles.title_zh: Coco Gauff Says Racist Abuse Has Been ‘Draining’ at China Open
articles.content_orig:
Coco Gauff says online racist abuse has left her feeling exhausted as she lost to Elise Mertens in the China Open.
The world number four, a Black American, turned in an uncharacteristically listless performance in Beijing on Wednesday, double-faulting eight times as she went down 6-3, 6-3 to her Belgian opponent.
Gauff, 22, was playing a day after she called out the “insane” amount of abuse she had received on the internet following her win over Chinese teenager Sun Xinran in the previous round.
“It has been kind of draining. I’m not going to lie,” Gauff said of the impact of the online comments.
“But I just turn off my phone and move on. There’s nothing you can do.”
Asked about the match, she said: “I think I just didn’t play well. I think I wasn’t moving well.
“There were a lot of things I didn’t do well. I thought Elise played well on the bigger points.”
During her previous match in Beijing, against Sun, Gauff requested a video review over flickering LED lights on the stadium’s advertising hoardings.
The move prompted some boos from the crowd. The umpire agreed to have the point replayed, and Gauff went on to win 7-5, 6-1.
Early on Tuesday, Gauff wrote on X: “Hey everyone, you can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist.”
She was responding to a post that contained a racial slur.
“The amount of racist comments and messages I’ve received in the last few hours is insane,” she wrote.
Gauff also clarified that she challenged the point before Sun had returned the ball, when she noticed the lights flicker for a second time.
Asked about the incident, a spokesperson for the Women’s Tennis Association, the global governing body, said it was “appalled by the racial abuse directed at Coco Gauff” and that it was “in contact with her to offer our full support”.
It added in a statement to the AFP news agency that there was “no place for racism, discrimination, or abuse in tennis”, and that it was “seeking action” against the abusive content.
Gauff, who won the Beijing title in 2024 and made the semifinals last year, was popular among fans during the tournament.
A group of supporters in the largely empty stadium tried to encourage her into a comeback on Wednesday.
Mertens was undeterred as she punched her ticket for a quarterfinal clash against Iga Swiatek.
The world number 19 called Gauff an “incredible player”, adding: “I knew it was going to be a very tough match.”
She dedicated her win to her coach, who is also her boyfriend.
Earlier, Swiatek swept aside American teenager Iva Jovic 6-1, 6-3 in one hour and 35 minutes.
“I had it under control from the beginning,” said the Polish world number nine. “I feel like I’m improving every day.”
China’s Zheng Qinwen is due to face 118th-ranked Alina Charaeva later on Wednesday.
Ukraine’s Elina Svitolina, the sixth seed, will play American Ann Li.

articles.title_orig: China’s thorium-229 nuclear clock beats Vienna’s on stability, studies show
articles.title_zh: China’s thorium-229 nuclear clock beats Vienna’s on stability, studies show
articles.content_orig:
Chinese and European teams in ‘fierce but friendly’ competition to develop the next-generation timepieces
Initial results from the world’s first two working nuclear clocks indicate that China’s timepiece is about six times as stable as the one in Vienna, according to papers published this week by the journal Nature.
The clocks were developed independently but both the Chinese team, led by Tsinghua University in Beijing, and the researchers at Vienna’s TU Wien used thorium-229 nuclei embedded in crystals to keep time by the steady rhythm of the atom’s core, rather than the electrons whirling around it, as in atomic clocks.
When Nature reported in June that the two teams had separately developed the radical new devices, Thorsten Schumm, a member of the European team, said that “now we have a fierce but friendly global competition”.
According to the latest papers, the Beijing scientists also showed that two crystals grown separately kept the same time – a sign such clocks could be reliably reproduced, they said. Meanwhile, the Vienna team used its clock to hunt for dark matter, without success.

articles.title_orig: Trump/Xi Summit: Deepening Crises and Confrontation Behind “Friendship Show”
articles.title_zh: Trump/Xi Summit: Deepening Crises and Confrontation Behind “Friendship Show”
articles.content_orig:
October 5, 2026 Per-Ake Westerlund, ISA International Political Committee
Xi Jinping’s 3-day state visit to Washington was an inferior, even emptier re-run of Trump’s visit to Beijing in May. Two imperialist superpower tyrants met and avoided everything important. Wars, climate catastrophe and AI were set aside for salutes, dinners and pandas. It was a “nothing burger”, Edgard D. Kagan at CSIS commented.
The event says a lot about world developments today. For both sides, it was about hiding crises that have deepened further since May, pretending everything is under control, and winning time in order to prepare for inevitable and sharper confrontations. The two presidents underlined each other’s “greatness” for their domestic audiences, including their opposition.
The only real agreement was to meet twice more this year (at the APEC summit in Shenzhen and G20 in Miami). This unique pace of meetings underlines both the fragile world situation and the continuing need of both “strong men” to promote each other’s importance. So too does the unique red carpet welcome Xi received from Trump. Reports say the actual talks between the two only lasted 90 minutes of the three day visit.
The meeting offered no “common global leadership”. Under the surface of incredible and hypocritical flattery, talk about friendship and peace, there is a continued aggressive imperialist build-up. As the Economist commented, “the main mission of American and Chinese commanders is to prepare to fight and win a conflict with one another, most probably over Taiwan”.
Since May, almost nothing has happened regarding the agreements which they claimed to have made at their previous face-to-face summit in Beijing.In fact since May, both regimes have taken new measures against each other – for example new blacklistings and restrictions against companies with military links. Trump is frustrated that Chinese exports of rare earths are only two thirds of what was agreed. Beijing protested when Washington threatened sanctions against countries trading with Iran this summer, of which China is by far the most important. The US also has ongoing investigations that can lead to new sanctions. Both sides are investing heavily in AI, the main ongoing arms and technological race between them.
None of these issues were dealt with during Xi’s visit. What was officially reported – as in May in two separate statements with differing content – was mostly a repeat of the talks in May. The ‘Board of Investment’ and the ‘Board of Trade’ launched in May have yet to do anything.
In May, Trump agreed to lift tariffs on $30 billion worth of “non-sensitive” Chinese exports. This was now repeated, but classified as “favourable treatment” rather than non-tariffs. This time it mentions trade in both directions so the value is raised to $60 billion. It includes 1,619 US items, featuring agricultural products “as well as whales and dolphins for breeding”. 77 non-sensitive Chinese items are listed, including clay pigeons for shooting ( Financial Times 29 September).
China’s purchase of 200 Boeing planes has still not progressed, or been increased as Trump predicted, but imports of US soybeans have been fulfilled. Another repeat was the Thucydides Trap theme which was raised once more by Xi, to underline his thesis of China as a rising power, one of two great powers.
The two sides’ statements from the meeting are selective and contradictory. Iran, despite being Trump’s largest crisis, was not high on the agenda, due to low expectations. The statements only repeated that Iran should not develop nuclear arms, which is Tehran’s official position, and a general stance against tolls on seafare.
One report says that “Unlike the White House fact sheet issued after that meeting [in May], this latest one does not reaffirm a shared call to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. More notably, there is no mention of possible reductions in Chinese purchases of Iranian crude or promises to stop providing Iranian companies with geospatial data and satellite imagery, both of which the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is reportedly using to attack commercial and military shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and to launch precision strikes on US military bases in the Middle East “
The US has also backed off from its previous threats to severely sanction countries trading with Iran, which would target China first and foremost. It is of course also in the interest of the CCP regime to calm the energy crisis, as was also shown in its recent statement against the threat of closure of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. Iran is an ally of China, but Beijing’s relations with the US are more important. Xi Jinping was welcomed with a red carpet, while the same B2-bombers used against Iran paid tribute in the sky above.
Washington claims that Trump raised the need to increase China’s exports of rare earths, but Beijing’s statement does not mention rare earths at all. In turn, Beijing’s account states that Xi raised Taiwan, arguing Trump should oppose independence, but the White House readout does not mention Taiwan. The Financial Times reported another “area where the two statements diverged, China said the US and Chinese militaries had agreed to ‘conclude a memorandum of understanding on crisis communication’. The Trump administration said that was not true”.
On trade, the fragile truce established in South Korea in November last year was prolonged to 10 January – a very short extension. Beijing has pushed for it to last the entire period of Trump’s presidency. The US, however, wants to keep all options open, including new tariffs and sanctions.
In May, the Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE) estimated the US’s average tariff on Chinese goods at 51.1 percent, covering all imports. In comparison, China’s average tariff on American goods was 32.6 percent. With the Supreme Court ruling to end some tariffs coming into force in July, China’s effective tariff rate, still the highest of all countries, was lowered to 22.8 percent, according to the University of Pennsylvania.
What the US seems to have won this time is coal exports to China of 10 million metric tons per year in 2027 and 2028, underlining the two powers’ common fear of energy crisis and neglect of the environmental consequences. China already produces 51 percent of the world’s coal. A vague “working group to discuss agricultural trade” was also to be established.
Again, Trump brought in tech billionaires such as Jeff Bezos (Amazon), OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk (SpaceX) and Jensen Huang (Nvidia). Xi, however, brought no Chinese CEOs to the event. Chinese CEOs would (correctly) not expect to achieve any deals in the US – with Alibaba, for example, on the US sanctions list – and in any case they would not have played any helpful role as decorations as the US CEOs do for Trump.
On AI, as expected nothing was reached apart from setting up a “dialogue” between the two powers. Trump, however, claimed that Xi accepted his latest renaming, to say “superintelligence” instead of AI. There is no such mention in the Chinese statements.
Chinese media, controlled by the CCP, underlined how Xi emphasised Taiwan as the main danger in their relations, pushing for Trump to replace the ambiguous position of “not supporting” Taiwan independence with “opposing” independence. This is another rerun of May. Trump, however, only said that they did not discuss it much, and that Xi knows his position. In the end, “Taiwan was not featured in either side’s end-of-summit readouts”.
However, what will worry governments in Taiwan, and Japan, is the report that “David Perdue, the US envoy to Beijing, said Trump has also asked Xi whether China was interested in buying US weapons. It was not clear when the comments were made, but they have drawn criticism in the US given China is viewed as its biggest military rival” ( Financial Times ).

articles.title_orig: Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos
articles.title_zh: Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos
articles.content_orig:
New ‘support and training centre’ prompts concern in region but China says it is ‘not directed at any third party’
Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new Chinese military facility in Laos , which opened last week and gives Beijing’s air force its first foothold in mainland south-east Asia.
Images provided by the commercial satellite provider Vantor show eight light attack aircraft positioned at Ban Keun airport alongside what appear to be more than a dozen military vehicles lined up in rows.
The planes’ shape matches that of the Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet, a two-seat trainer that can be deployed in combat to carry bombs. Laos is reported to have four such aircraft, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.
In a rare example of Beijing’s overseas military expansion, China opened what it said was a joint “support and training centre” at Ban Keun on 29 September.
The airport, about ⁠30 miles (50km) north of Vientiane, the capital of Laos, has been significantly expanded over the past year. Satellite images taken months ago show farmland and dirt paths where there are now new buildings and a paved runway.
Aside from its island bases in the South China Sea, Beijing does not have a significant network of military outposts in other countries, and the Laos airbase would be its first facility in another country capable of handling fighter jets.
The new satellite images, taken a day after the announcement and first reported by Reuters, show extensive construction work that appears to be focused on a future runway extension, which could make the airport capable of handling larger planes such as bombers.
In its announcement last week, China’s defence ministry said the new centre would “help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots” and was not “directed against any third party”.
Governments will be watching closely for signs of deployments or the installation of defence equipment that may serve wider military ambitions. After the announcement, the Singapore-based security analyst Collin Koh said it “may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA [People’s Liberation Army] overseas base in south-east Asia”.
Over the past two decades, China has built up an extensive network of outposts on islands in the disputed South China Sea, including airbases with air defence installations. Otherwise, its navy’s sole overseas military base is a logistics base in Djibouti, on the coast of the Horn of Africa .
The Laos agreement follows a similar programme established in Cambodia, at the Ream naval base on the Gulf of Thailand, although that facility has no runway.
After years of speculation and denials , China announced in April last year that it had created the “joint logistics and training” facility in Cambodia. It said the centre would support the two militaries in “conducting regional counter-terrorism, disaster prevention and mitigation, humanitarian assistance, joint training and other operations”.
US forces are believed to have used Ban Keun airport in Laos during covert military operations at the height of the Vietnam war in the 1960s and 1970s. Its development will be monitored by Vietnam, which maintains disputes with China over the South China Sea, and Thailand, which shares a border with Laos.
After the announcement last week, Thailand’s defence ministry spokesperson said Bangkok considered itself a close partner of both Laos and China and saw it as Vientiane’s sovereign right to decide whether to grant permission for a Chinese base.
“Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments and how the matter proceeds, particularly with regard to building mutual trust,” said R Adm Surasant Kongsiri.
China’s government did not mention sending aircraft to Laos in its initial announcement, while the government of Laos has not commented on the project.
The US-based Institute for the Study of War has described the Laos base as the “first PLA overseas military facility focused on air power”. In its assessment, the thinktank said the base was “not yet equipped to provide the PLA with the ability to execute major combat operations, unlike US military bases”.
It said the base would give the Chinese military alternate routes to access to the South China Sea and strategic air routes.
Reuters contributed to this report

articles.content_orig:
Stand for Israel | October 7, 2026
Three years ago today, Israel and her people endured the most horrific acts of terror in the nation’s modern history on October 7, 2023. The Holy Land held its National Day of Remembrance earlier this week, but Jews and Christians in the U.S. and around the world are taking today to remember the more than 1,200 victims, the 251 people who were kidnapped, and the countless lives and communities that continue to be affected.
JNS reports that Israel’s envoy to the Christian world George Deek praised the Flags of Fellowship movement ahead of the annual Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit.
Three years after October 7, to see millions of Christians around the world publicly raise Israel’s flag is a powerful reminder that friendship can speak louder than hatred. More than 5.2 million Israeli flags, over 4,375 churches, universities and organizations, in 14 countries. WOW.
At a time when Israel and the Jewish people have faced extraordinary hatred, millions of Christians are choosing something different: friendship, remembrance and solidarity. I am deeply grateful to the International Fellowship of Christians and Jews, to Yael Eckstein, and to every pastor, church and community taking part in this remarkable initiative.
To our Christian friends around the world: thank you for standing with Israel. We see you. We appreciate you. And we will never take your friendship for granted.
The Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit will run through October 11, coinciding with Flags of Fellowship. More than 1,000 Christian leaders and influencers from 117 countries arrived in Israel on Monday for the second consecutive year of the summit. Around 300 of the participants are between the ages of 18 and 29. Summit founder Mike Evans says he hopes young Christians will see Israel for themselves and hear directly from those affected by October 7.
Much like Flags of Fellowship, the Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit carries the powerful message that Israel does not stand alone, building connections based on truth, courage, and a determination to confront anti-Semitism.
The Fellowship and our supporters pray for the families and remember the victims of October 7 alongside the 4,375 churches and synagogues around the world participating in Flags of Fellowship and the Christian ambassadors who have just arrived in Israel.

articles.title_orig: Rising seas threaten the world’s migratory shorebirds
articles.title_zh: Rising seas threaten the world’s migratory shorebirds
articles.content_orig:
Birds undertake some of the world’s most impressive migrations , travelling hundreds to thousands of kilometres every year in search of safe breeding grounds and seasonally abundant food resources. For many birds, migration is the key to their success . However, migration can also make species more vulnerable to threats.
Shorebirds — species that include sandpipers, plovers and oystercatchers — live and migrate along the world’s coastlines. Over the last several decades, coastal development has led to the loss of shorebird habitats in many areas of the world, driving population declines in multiple species . Now, a new threat is emerging: climate change-driven sea-level rise.
But how exactly does sea-level rise impact shorebirds, and just how serious is this threat?
Our new study reviews the evidence from 37 published papers to provide the first comprehensive overview of the threat of sea-level rise to the world’s shorebirds. Long story short: things aren’t looking good.
Shorebirds — as their name suggests — live along the shore, relying primarily on coastal ecosystems like  beaches, salt marshes and tidal flats. As sea levels rise, these vital habitats shrink.
Some coastal ecosystems may persist in the face of sea-level rise by moving inland with the rising waters, but this isn’t always possible. More than half of the world’s largest cities are within 100 kilometres of a coast , meaning that the presence of coastal infrastructure often blocks these pathways.
This leads to a phenomenon known as coastal squeeze — where ecosystems are increasingly squeezed between the rising waters and an inland barrier (such as dikes and seawalls built to protect homes and businesses), leading to decreases in habitat.
Loss of habitat has obvious implications for migratory shorebirds: less access to food, less space for nesting and more competition with other individuals.
But habitat loss isn’t the only threat to these species. Sea-level rise may also impact shorebirds in different ways, leading to changes in prey distribution , reproductive success , feeding time and many other factors.
Among the 37 studies that we examined, 21 predicted negative impacts of sea-level rise on shorebird habitats such as declines in habitat area or quality, while 17 predicted negative impacts on shorebird populations or individuals such as decreased survival or abundance.
Sea-level rise is expected to drive substantial habitat loss at many sites of international importance for migratory shorebirds. These include San Francisco Bay and Humboldt Bay in the United States, the Colorado River Delta and Marismas Nacionales in Mexico and the Yellow Sea region in East Asia, each of which supports 150,000 to more than one million shorebirds annually.
Habitat loss at these kinds of migratory bottleneck sites where large numbers of shorebirds congregate over a short period of time may hit populations particularly hard. Because so many birds funnel through these sites during migration, habitat loss in these areas may impact multiple species and entire populations. This means these sites must be a priority for conservation.
Maintaining coastal ecosystems and protecting them from the threat of sea-level rise will be essential for the survival of thriving shorebird populations. But coastal ecosystems aren’t only important for shorebirds. They also support thousands of other species and provide valuable ecosystem services such as coastal protection, water filtration and carbon storage.
In order to preserve these habitats and the species that depend on them, governments will need to make a serious effort to mitigate the impacts of coastal squeeze. Rather than continuing to armour our shorelines, decision makers should prioritize solutions that will protect human communities while also benefitting coastal ecosystems .
The shape that these actions take may vary from place to place. In some areas, it may be necessary to relocate coastal infrastructure to give ecosystems space to move inland as sea levels rise — an approach referred to as “managed retreat.” In other areas, scientists and practitioners are looking at how we can use sediment recovered from dredging to enhance or create new habitats.
However we choose to respond to sea-level rise, urgent action will be required to preserve shorebirds and their fascinating migrations for generations to come.

articles.title_orig: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.title_zh: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.content_orig:
The victim was working at the anti-plague institute in the Siberia city of Irkutsk
US President Donald Trump has said he will speak with Vladimir Putin soon about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia.
"So far we are in very deep discussions," Trump said, adding that he would be able to report on his talks with the Russian leader "probably" on Thursday. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no phone call had been scheduled.
Russian officials say they are investigating the cause of the 28-year-old's death and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague. They insist there is no risk of an epidemic.
Mongolia has ordered "surveillance measures" on its border, AFP reports, while Lithuania has made preparations for any possible case.
Pneumonic plague is a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for transparency from Russia.
"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Putin's spokesman said Russia's reporting of the death to the WHO was in line with standard practice, and accused the media of reporting "false information".
The US has issued a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting additional information. Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a request.
Reports first emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation in Siberia's Irkutsk region following the death.
The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier.
Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after either breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
As the US and the WHO sought more information, the country's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, issued a statement saying "there are no epidemic risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region".
It said more than 90% of the people who had been in contact with the victim had "completed medical observation" and "no health disorders associated with infectious pathology were detected".
Neighbouring Mongolia's government has ordered "health surveillance" measures on its border with Russia, AFP news agency reported. The country's health ministry said it would "maintain continuous surveillance and monitoring to prevent potential risks".
This was a precautionary measure, it said, adding "the current risk level is low."
Lithuania's health ministry said it has made preparations to manage any possible case in the country.
Laboratory testing is available, patients would be isolated in infectious disease hospitals, contacts would be identified, and the country has the stocks of medicines suitable for treatment, according to Nerija Kaulakien, an adviser at the Ministry of Health's Communications Division, in an interview with ELTA news agency.
There was no evidence of "an increased risk of plague" at the moment, she said.
In the immediate wake of the laboratory worker's death, Russia's health watchdog had issued a statement saying the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology" and that testing found "no microorganisms related to her professional activities".
However, after this announcement, a pro-government federal news outlet deleted five posts mentioning a possible plague case, and authorities in the town of Baikalsk deleted a message advising against travel to Shelekhov because of a possible plague infection.
Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed.
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.
People can be infected through:
contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials
the inhalation of respiratory particles
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.
The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death .
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago.

articles.content_orig:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
SAN FRANCISCO—In what is sure to be a jam-packed presentation, Microsoft finally seems ready to talk more about its Nvidia RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra , along with its visions for Copilot and Windows . Between Computex and Build earlier this year, it's clear that Redmond has been cooking up some fresh ( and likely expensive ) ideas about personal computing in the age of AI and agents , and we can't wait to hear more.
Whatever Microsoft reveals at its surprise fall event, which starts on Wednesday, Oct. 7, at 10 a.m. PT (1 p.m. EST), we'll be covering it all live. Make sure to tune in early and check back often, though, as we'll be updating this story with from-the-ground insights and deeper analysis throughout the week. You can also watch the event live from the Windows YouTube channel, starting at 12:45 EST.
The announcement of this event was somewhat unexpected, so no one knows for sure what to expect. That said, we're pretty confident that it will include plenty of news about RTX Spark PCs (including the Surface Laptop Ultra) since Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is making an appearance. articles.title_zh: World leaders solemnly mark 3 years since Oct. 7, as Hamas and Iran celebrate anniversary
articles.content_orig:

The world changed when Hamas attacked Israelis on Oct. 7, 2023 , catalyzing devastating conflict throughout the region . But within Israel, political sentiments have changed surprisingly little.
To some, the attack fulfilled long-term right-wing warnings that Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza would yield disaster; and the attack was incontrovertible proof that Palestinians will never live in peace with Israel.
Israeli left-wingers, for their part, have long held that a festering military rule over Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, and failure to reach peace, would inevitably lead to violent conflagration. For them, Oct. 7 only proved that they had been right all along.
The standoff raises crucial questions. In three years since Oct. 7, how has the attack changed Israeli society? And how will the answer affect upcoming elections in Israel?
To be sure, there have been cataclysmic changes in Israel, and the Middle East at large, since Oct. 7. The war in Gaza that began that day has become Israel’s longest war. A relatively stable ceasefire with Lebanon from 2006 to 2023 ended when Hezbollah, a Shi’a militia group, fired on Israel the day after Hamas’ attack; after multiple escalations since then, the current ceasefire is precarious. Israel and the U.S. have waged two full-blown wars with Iran, and the Middle East is still threatened by spin-off conflicts.
The losses Israelis suffered on Oct. 7 and since then have affected the country collectively and profoundly. For two years, many Israelis went from demonstration to demonstration demanding that their government prioritize a deal with Hamas to release Israeli hostages. Hundreds of thousands have spent the last three years in and out of active reserve duty.
Since 2023, Israel has seen record levels of emigration and growing international isolation. Sixty-one percent of Israelis told pollsters for the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) that the national mood is poor .
Moreover, the destruction of Palestinian life and society , still ongoing , will one day force a terrible reckoning within Israel.
What’s less visible, and more surprising, is what has stayed the same. Israelis’ attitudes towards Palestinians, occupation, and conflict have become more extreme. But I would argue that Israeli public opinion today says much more about how Israel had changed prior to Oct. 7. The change in national attitudes since that fateful day has been moderate and consistent with what came before.
In December 2022, almost a year before Oct. 7, support for peace through a two-state solution hit a historic low. In the joint Palestinian-Israeli survey I conduct together with colleagues at Tel Aviv University and the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, support stood at 39% of Israelis that year—the lowest since the 1990s. Among Jewish respondents, just 34% supported a two-state solution, and 37% believed Israel should permanently annex the West Bank while Palestinians would have limited rights.
When we conducted the study again in mid-2024, Jews were twice as likely to support a single, Israeli-dominated unequal state as they were to support two states.
Palestinian attitudes in 2022 were similar. Just one-third supported two states. Both sides showed a mirror-image majority who distrusted the other. In surveys by the IDI from that same time, 59% of Jewish Israelis defined themselves as right-wing; just 12% said they were left-wing.
What changed after Oct. 7? This July, the Tel Aviv University Peace Index survey found that support for two states stood at 31%, an eight-point decline in the four years since 2022. Now, IDI surveys find that just over 60% of Israeli Jews describe themselves as right-wing, just a few points higher than late 2022.
Israel has changed, but this change began years before Oct. 7 2023. In 2010 , no fewer than 71% of Israelis supported a two-state solution in the joint surveys. The years that followed were plagued by stagnation and dissipation of any peace process, regular wars with Hamas, and a heavily nationalist government in Israel. It stands to reason that these phenomena pushed Israeli society further to the right. Support for the two-state solution eroded slowly, then rapidly by the end of the decade.
That shift was self-reinforcing: the more right-wing Israelis became (primarily the Jewish population), the more elected leaders took ever-more radical positions such as supporting settlement expansion and de facto annexation in the West Bank. In 2019, Prime Minister Netanyahu began referring to extending sovereignty over parts of the West Bank, or de jure annexation . The current government accelerated those processes drastically.
Study after study shows that Arab citizens of Israel have remained the strongest supporters of peace, before and after the current wars. But with Jewish Israeli and Palestinian attitudes so dismal in the years before Oct. 7, the chances of resurgent violence almost seemed inevitable.
In other words, most Israelis did not radically transform their worldview after Oct. 7. In fact, hardline political trends were among the many factors contributing to the terrible escalation to begin with.
Another thing that hasn’t changed in Israel during the last three years of war: hopes for peace. The number of Israeli Jews who self-describe as left-wing has barely shifted. In a May survey for the Institute for National Security Studies, about 20% of the total population, Jews and Arabs, define themselves as left-wing, and a similar share typically say they are centrist. These groups embrace a commitment to democracy, liberal values, separation of religion and state, and reject the religious fundamentalism of the current government.
The left remains committed to peace via diplomacy and Palestinian self-determination. In a mid-2025 survey I conducted for a peace organization called A Land for All, where I am also an active member, the large majority of self-defined left-wing Israelis, and nearly half of centrists, supported a basic two-state solution.
Do peace attitudes even matter, when there is no peace process? That may be theoretical for now, but elections aren’t. Israelis will be voting on Oct. 27. Polls show the voters deeply divided , just as they were in the elections held between 2019 and 2022.
Netanyahu’s far-right coalition is not doing well. Nearly all polls show his coalition parties well below their actual result in 2022. And most mainstream polls show a consistent majority for today’s opposition parties.
At first glance, these shifts might seem antithetical. Aren’t these ideological and electoral trends moving in contradictory directions: more right-wing, but a majority against the current government?
It turns out that even the Israeli electoral contradiction is not new. During the five elections from 2019 through 2022, a majority of Israelis were right-wing and voted for right-wing parties. But to form a coalition, some of those parties no longer supported Netanyahu and refused to join a coalition under his leadership. Netanyahu therefore commanded only about half the seats in parliament following four of these cycles. Neither side had a clear or firm coalition majority, and the country was thrown into electoral turmoil five times over.
But if all mainstream polls show the anti-Netanyahu parties winning, including right-wing opposition parties, shouldn’t that mean a decisive outcome against him this time? Not quite: no poll shows Israel’s Jewish, Zionist parties reaching a majority in October.
And in Israel’s right-wing, populist discourse, the main opposition party leaders opposed to Netanyahu now, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman, with similar statements from frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot , insist that parties representing Arab citizens must not be part of a coalition after Oct. 7. Two seaside resorts in New England are among the best on the planet, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers.
The travel publication released a list of the 50 best resorts in the world on Tuesday, part of its 39th Annual Readers’ Choice Awards , and Chatham Bars Inn in Chatham ranked No. 18. Weekapaug Inn in Westerly, R.I. ranked No. 28.
Chatham Bars Inn , which was also named the No. 1 resort in New England , is “a benchmark of luxury on the Cape,” Conde Nast Traveler wrote.
“If you’re looking for a full-service resort with all the bells and whistles and then some, this is it, including an eight-acre private farm to stock the resort’s numerous dining and drinking outlets; one of the better spas on the Cape; an expansive pool deck with F&B service; a private quarter-mile beachfront; tennis courts with lessons available; and a 24-hour gym,” wrote the publication.
Resort officials celebrated on social media , writing, “Thank you to our incredible team and to our guests and supporters who voted for us. We’re grateful to be recognized alongside so many remarkable destinations.”
Weekapaug Inn, also named the No. 2 resort in New England , is a historic getaway in Rhode Island.
“A recently renovated legendary seaside inn on the National Register of Historic Places, the 27-room, six-suite Weekapaug Inn is a three-hour drive from New York and less than two from Boston—ideal for a quick weekend jaunt,” wrote Conde Nast Traveler .
Visitors enjoy guided nature walks, golf, tennis, and boating expeditions in historic vessels, noted the publication.
Officials at Weekapaug Inn also shared their excitement on social media , writing, “Thank you to the Condé Nast Traveler readers who voted, and to our incredible teams for truly delivering the best of service, cuisine, and luxury, year after year. We hope to share our award-winning experiences with you soon.”
The No. 1 resort in the world is Cheval Blanc Seychelles, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers.
This year, Conde Nast Traveler readers cast 798,867 votes for the annual awards, determining the very best in hotels, resorts, spas, airlines, and more worldwide. The results will be featured in the magazine’s November issue.

articles.title_orig: A UMass study has revealed two of the world’s loudest birds. Here’s what they sound like.
articles.title_zh: A UMass study has revealed two of the world’s loudest birds. Here’s what they sound like.
articles.content_orig:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
University of Massachusetts Amherst biologists have discovered two contenders for the world’s loudest birds, both from Brazil.
The bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema are louder than jackhammers and may just be the loudest birds in the world, according to a study published in Evolution by UMass professor Jeff Podos and his former graduate student João Menezes.
This isn’t the first groundbreaking discovery for Podos. In fact, his research established a Guinness World Record in 2019 when he discovered that the Amazon’s white bellbird had the world’s loudest bird call, louder than a revving chainsaw.
The latest discovery is the result of Podos and Menezes’s years of ongoing research to understand the role evolutionary biology plays in how birds communicate with each other. Their research aims to solve the mystery of why some birds are so much louder than others, and whether there are certain physical traits that can predict their volume.
Menezes said it’s difficult to measure how loud a bird call is in the field, and there’s little data available. But using cutting-edge tools, Podos and Menezes have gathered reliable amplitude data on 123 species throughout Massachusetts and Brazil, 113 of which had never before had their volume catalogued.
“We’ve been able to vastly increase the number of species for which there is amplitude data,” Podos said. “This is basic, foundational research that no one else has managed to do on this scale, and it points to all sorts of other questions that would be fun to follow up.”
Podos and Menezes discovered there’s a 58-decibel range in the volume of bird calls, from the hummingbird, whose calls are 64 decibels and about the volume of a normal conversation, to bare-throated bellbirds and red-legged seriemas, who register at over 120 decibels.
They found that the loudest birds are typically bigger, with wider beak openings and bulky muscles that may allow greater air compression for explosive volume. But Podos and Menezes said there’s still a lot unknown about how birds communicate.
“We now know some of the hows,” Menezes said. “Bigger bodies and wider beaks. But we’ve yet to discover the whys, and we probably need much more data from many more species to be able to tease out what’s going on on the ecological and evolutionary front.”

Stocks fell on Wednesday as pressure continued to build in the bond market, pushing Treasury yields to levels not seen in more than two decades .
The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 503 points, or 1%, while the S&P 500 shed 0.6%. The Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.7%.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield climbed more than 8 basis points to trade at 5.356%. The yield reached its highest level since April 2002 . The 30-year bond yield gained more than 8 basis points to 5.725%. It had hit its highest level since May 2002.
The moves come ahead of a planned auction by the Treasury Wednesday, in which it's planning to sell $39 billion of 10-year notes.
Bank stocks dropped as investors feared higher interest rates would hinder lending activity. Shares of Goldman Sachs moved down nearly 3%, while Citigroup pulled back more than 2%. Others such as Bank of America , Wells Fargo and JPMorgan shed more than 1%.
Technology stocks also came under pressure amid worries that higher borrowing costs would limit the artificial intelligence buildout. CrowdStrike shares were lower by 3%, while Palo Alto Networks and Meta Platforms each lost more than 2%.
Meanwhile, U.S. crude prices also crept back toward $90 per barrel. International Brent crude futures , meanwhile, traded nearly 1% higher at around $101 per barrel. Those moves led yields, which took a breather in the previous session, to resume the recent surge that drove them to multiyear highs.
The S&P 500 closed above 7,800 for the first time on Tuesday, led by gains in chipmakers. Bond yields also eased, giving equities a boost.
"Stocks have gotten cheaper since January which is ironic, since we're hitting all-time highs," said Nancy Tengler, CEO and CIO of Laffer Tengler. "I don't mind multiple compression because it tells me that this bull market is sustainable and it elongates it. I like where we sit for this bull market, and earnings growth does ultimately drive stock price performance."
Investors are awaiting the minutes of the Federal Reserve's last meeting in September, at which the U.S. central bank raised interest rates for the first time since 2023. Minutes are set to shed light on how monetary policymakers are thinking about economic conditions.
Shares of Webull tanked 20% on Wednesday after a bipartisan congressional panel found that the digital investing platform has deep ties to China's government, CNBC reported .
The committee stated the company's structural connection to China represents a national security threat to U.S. finance.
A Webull spokesperson said the committee's report has "significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions."
Webull's investment platform has 28 million global users and offers investment services in 18 markets around the globe.
— Paulina Likos and Eamon Javers
Gold hit a low of 4,091.2 on Wednesday, reaching the lowest level since Aug. 3, when it traded as low as 4,074.
The move lower is helped in part by a strong dollar which make dollar-denominated metals more expensive to foreign buyers.
Gold has not traded below 4,000 since July 20 when gold hit a low of 3,986.
Gold Miners are down 3.85%, on pace for worst day since Sep. 28, when the GDX fell 5.36%
Silver also hit a low of $59.23, the lowest level since Aug. 4, when silver traded as low as $58.18.
— Gina Francolla and Paulina Likos
The three major averages began Wednesday's session in the red.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 340 points, or 0.7%, just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the S&P 500 dropped 0.4%. The Nasdaq Composite declined 0.5%.
Morgan Stanley upgraded Gold Fields to Overweight, saying the stock's underperformance has created an attractive risk-reward setup.
Gold Fields has lagged global gold peers by about 16% this year. But according to Morgan Stanley's analyst Christopher Nicholson much of the uncertainty around its Tarkwa mining lease is already priced in.
"We think Tarkwa lease risk is largely priced; in addition, a potential Northern Star deal looks accretive on a pro forma basis. We update earnings estimates and price targets on the back of our latest price deck – the risk-reward for gold skews upwards," said Nicholson.
Overall, the analyst remains bullish on the gold , naming the yellow metal as its top commodity pick and forecasting an average price of $5,050 an ounce in 2027. Nicholson said gold could benefit from concerns around government debt, potential intervention to cap bond yields, swings in oil prices and continued central-bank buying.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury note rose nearly 8 basis points to hit a high of 5.350% on Wednesday, officially topping its high from Monday.
The marks the highest level since April 3, 2002, when it reached 5.379%.

Constellation Brands shares fell 5% even after the company reported better-than-expected results for its fiscal second quarter.
The beer distributor earned an $3.74 per share on revenue of $2.63 billion. Analysts expected a profit of $3.56 per share on revenue of $2.54 billion.
That said, beer operating margins decreased by 160 basis points year on year. Depletions, a key demand metric for the company, fell slightly from the year-earlier period as well.

"The U.S. has been a reliable supplier to the world at a time when it needs it," Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC's " Squawk Box Europe " in an exclusive interview on Wednesday.
"And I think it would be unwise for the U.S. to create questions in the minds of our allies and our partners as to whether or not we will be there with reliable supply when times are difficult — and so, there are other options," he added.

"While the market overall has been fairly subdued, property prices have so far proved resilient during a period of higher mortgage rates, which has been driven by changing expectations around the future path of Base Rate," Andrew Asaam, mortgages director at Lloyds, said in the data release. "That's mirrored in wider economic data, with household spending holding up better than many expected despite energy and other cost pressures arising from the Middle East conflict."
Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 0.92% lower at 70,035.71, and the broader Topix fell 0.70% to 4,154.11.
South Korea's Kospi declined nearly 2% to 6,803.90, while the small-cap Kosdaq lost 2.34% to 898.43.
Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 ended flat at 8,727.70.

Mining and tech stocks led losses, while Germany's DAX — down 0.9% — notched the biggest decline among major regional bourses.

Meanwhile, French and Italian 10-year government bond yields rose by 8 basis points. Japanese bonds bucked the trend, with yields trading marginally lower.

Blachnicka improved on her previous podium result, stepping up from bronze in Žilina, Slovakia, to silver in Leipzig.
Ukraine’s Mariia Shymkova, who won silver in Žilina, returned to the podium in third place. She clocked 7.58 to narrowly beat teammate Sofiia Tulchynska’s 7.63.

Former German foreign intelligence agency boss August Hanning appeared before a federal judge in the western city of Karlsruhe on Wednesday following his arrest on espionage and treason charges Tuesday.
He has been ordered to remain in detention ahead of his trial, according to federal prosecutors.
Manfred D., Hanning's former chief of staff at the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) , was also detained.
Manfred D. is accused of having stolen secret documents and turned these over to Hanning, who, as a private-sector security adviser, in turn reportedly sold the secret documents to an as yet unnamed foreign spy agency or agencies.

Investigators estimate the two stole and potentially passed on more than 2,000 secret documents between 2010 and 2023. Federal investigators say it is unclear how much information was stolen and to whom it was sold.
Hanning ran the BND, Germany's foreign intelligence service, from 1998 until 2005 before becoming state secretary at the Federal Interior Ministry and then entering private business as a security adviser.
The issue has raised serious questions about the trustworthiness of Germany's intelligence agencies and shocked politicians into action as they claim not enough is being done to ensure high-ranking officials do not abuse their experience when transitioning to jobs in the private sector.
Although it is currently not known who Hanning's potential customers were, Germany's weekly Der Spiegel magazine on Wednesday named Azerbaijan as one. articles.title_orig: 11 Places to See the World's Most Magnificent Wildlife Migrations
articles.title_zh: 11 Places to See the World's Most Magnificent Wildlife Migrations
articles.content_orig:
Seeing an immense number  of creatures assembled in one place is a phenomenon worth travelling for. Here’s when, where and how to experience some of nature’s wildest gatherings.
Seeing any animal in the wild is a privilege — but seeing huge numbers is something else. For a start, it’s both humbling and heartening to encounter any species in abundance. It’s also genuinely exciting. When big groups of creatures seasonally cluster in one place, there’s always something to watch — from courting and mating to fighting or family-raising. It may be a sensory assault, too: noise, tumult, pungent smells, crashing waters, mad flurries of dust. And where masses gather to move together, hungry predators may lurk, adding a macabre but fascinating dimension. Here, we’ve picked the most dramatic migrations through the year and around the globe.
When to go: December to March
How does an insect the weight of a paperclip make a journey of 3,000 miles? That’s the feat of the extraordinary monarch butterfly, which somehow flutters from its summer breeding grounds — spread across Canada and the American northeast — to a patch of oyamel fir forest in the highlands west of Mexico City. Most only survive for a month or so but, in autumn, a generation emerges that lives eight times as long, capable of making this perilous trip. How they know where to go is a mystery — the butterflies that migrate are the great-great-grandchildren of those that left Mexico the previous spring. No matter, the results are spectacular: millions upon millions of orange-black wings blanketing trees, raining like tickertape. The Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, in the mountains of Michoacán state, is home to more than half of the overwintering colonies of the monarch butterfly’s eastern population. The sanctuary of El Rosario is easiest to reach; lesser-visited Sierra Chincua can be explored on horseback. The colourful, cobblestoned Mineral de Angangueo makes a good base.
The Indigenous Sámi of Europe’s far north work to their own calendar. Their year has eight seasons, and giđđa (spring) means melting snows, fast-increasing daylight and reindeer on the move: around April, the animals start migrating from their inland pastures towards the coast for summer grazing. Norway has around 275,000 reindeer, some wild, but mostly semi-domesticated herds that are ushered across the country’s Arctic plateaus by Sámi families whose livelihoods have depended on the practice for generations. Finnmarksvidda, an empty vastness of low hills, glacial lakes, pine barrens, birch woods and bogs in northernmost Norway, is a Sámi stronghold, where a few operators offer the chance to join the herders on the move. Days are shaped by the reindeer and the weather, perhaps involving sledding, snowmobiling or feeding the animals, followed by sharing stories around the fire, feasting on Arctic fish and sleeping in lavvus (traditional tents). Seeing swathes of animals trot across the tundra is a treat; being immersed in Sámi culture is an even greater privilege.
A strange thing happens off the South African coast each winter in the Southern Hemisphere: sardines in their millions, maybe billions, swarm north from Cape Agulhas, following a cold current towards the Indian Ocean. Strange, because it doesn’t benefit the sardines at all. But it’s a bumper buffet for other creatures: dolphins, tuna, seals, sharks, orcas and whales, plus dive-bombing cormorants, gannets and gulls. The result is marine mayhem. The sardines become silvery shape-shifting bait balls, chased down by great gangs of hungry predators and pierced by an avian invasion from above. Fish numbers have plunged in recent decades and the Sardine Run has become less predictable, but it’s still known as one of Earth’s greatest shoals. Activity peaks off Eastern Cape province, with boat trips leaving from towns such as Port St Johns and Gqeberha (formerly Port Elizabeth, handy for Addo Elephant National Park, too). Diving amid this chaos is thrilling, if challenging; snorkellers can launch into the action more quickly. Or, stay on board to watch the feasting frenzy from above.
With their massive bills and bodies, capacious pouches and wide, powerful wings, pelicans look both immensely impressive and distinctly prehistoric. Come spring, around 32,000 of them — mostly great whites, plus a significant scoop of dalmatians, the biggest species — leave their winter hangouts and make for Europe’s largest natural wetland, the Danube Delta. This splurge of rivers, lakes, marshes, forest, sandbars and reedbeds spreads mostly across eastern Romania. It’s a paradise for the pelicans, as well as other birds such as herons, storks and white-tailed eagles. The pelicans begin arriving in March, but May is an ideal time to visit, when colonies are a-bustle, large pods gather for herd-fishing and adults are in full breeding splendour, their great gular pouches beaming bright-orange. June, on the other hand, is good for spying chicks, and July the time to go for sheer numbers. Navigate the delta on boat trips with licensed guides (mandatory for exploring core areas) or stay on a floating hotel for 24/7 avian action.
When to go: July to October
No migration is easy, but the journey of the Pacific Northwest salmon reads like a Greek tragedy. Born in fresh water, they head out to sea, mature for a few years, then navigate back to their natal streams using the earth’s magnetic fields and their own sense of smell. They battle against the flow, leaping rapids, dodging grizzlies and eagles, only to spawn — and then die. It’s a privilege to witness this fatal journey, either from the riverbank, as the fish fling themselves from the froth, or in the water amid the shoals. The town of Campbell River, on Vancouver Island’s east coast, is the self-proclaimed ‘salmon capital of the world’, and the top spot for snorkelling with the chinook, coho, chum, pink and sockeye fighting to return home. Floating in the swift current, you might see hundreds, even thousands, of salmon swim past — and possibly some bears hanging about. From the banks, you can watch salmon leaping two metres into the air, perhaps only to be snatched by those waiting bears. From mid-August to late October, the Homalco First Nation run bear-watching trips to Bute Inlet.

articles.title_orig: Jaguar unveils electric car in gamble on US tech millionaires
articles.title_zh: Jaguar unveils electric car in gamble on US tech millionaires
articles.content_orig:
Luxury carmaker Jaguar has launched its new all-electric vehicle, two years after the famed British company's controversial rebrand prompted a social media backlash.
The automotive manufacturer, which is owned by India's Tata Motors , unveiled the Type 01 model on Tuesday at an event in New York City, describing it as the "most technically advanced" and "most powerful and aerodynamic" Jaguar ever.
It marks a radical new direction for the company, which was criticized in November 2024 when it revealed a series of changes ahead of becoming a fully electric brand.
Jaguar posted a 30-second clip on X at the time which featured several models in brightly colored clothing and marketing slogans such as "live vivid", "delete ordinary" and "copy nothing."
Notably, the ad did not feature a car or the company's traditional cat logo. Among those to criticize the ad was Elon Musk , with the owner of the X social media platform asking : "Do you sell cars?"
Jaguar sought to defend the ad campaign, telling Sky News at the time that the company wanted "to be bold and disruptive."
Italy's Ferrari and Britain's Bentley have also launched their first EV models this year, seeking to test wealthy buyers' appetite for going electric as luxury carmakers seek to compete with cheaper Chinese car brands.
Jaguar's Type 01 has a starting price of £130,000 (roughly $172,000) in the U.K. and around $130,500 in the U.S., according to multiple media reports , which is significantly higher than previous comparable models.
Jaguar later confirmed to CNBC on Wednesday morning that the Type 01 model has a minimum price tag of $130,000 in North America.
The four-door "Grand Tourer" has an ultra-long bonnet, low roofline, frameless doors and a camera instead of a rear window. It has a range of up to 450 miles and can accelerate from 0-62 miles per hour in 3.2 seconds.
The launch of the model comes as Jaguar Land Rover continues its recovery from a cyberattack that forced the company to halt production last year, and one month after JLR announced it would cut 4,000 jobs as part of a major cost-cutting drive.
JLR CEO PB Balaji described the unveiling of Type 01 as the start of "an exciting new era" for Jaguar.
"Combining British heritage, bold creativity, advanced technology and groundbreaking engineering, it reflects our ambition to create objects of desire that will help us invite a new generation of clients into Jaguar's loyal and passionate customer base," Balaji said in a statement.

Nick Seibel, editor and publisher of the Silver City Daily Press, covers top stories each week in the Silver City Report. This week, he updates us on the horse that was infected with New World Screwworm, talks about a recent candidate forum, and more.
Susan Morée: You have an update for us on that poor horse that was infected with New World screw worm. How's the horse doing?
Nick Seibel: Yeah, well, I mean, the horse is recovering. You know, it was according to the veterinarians that treated the horse. The wound on the horse when they discovered it really didn't have the strong odor that's usually associated with that infestation. until they started to clean up the wound and found larvae deeper in the horse's tissue.
Yeah, it was unpleasant, but so far, no new cases reported in the area. Of course, there's an infestation zone, which is a 20 kilometer radius around where the horse was in Mimbres. There's a lot of sort of mystery around that particular infestation, because a lot of folks say, well, did the horse come from somewhere? But as it turns out, the horse had not left that property. Other animals that were on the property hadn't recently traveled on or off of the property. So a lot of mystery around how the fly got there to infect said horse. Generally, the experts say the flies travel at most about a mile or a mile and a half, but they can travel up to 10 miles per day. But not having had any other cases, we don't really know how that came to pass. So whether there's undetected infections that are out there, whether there's infestations in wild animals in the area. At the public meeting, the person from the state said that as far as they knew, the fly could have traveled in the cabin of a truck from somewhere else. You just don't know how that went down. But they are continuing with monitoring. They've got that infestation zone where you're supposed to have permission to transport animals in or out of there. They're also releasing sterile flies throughout the area to try to address the potential for flies out there in the wild and make sure that this doesn't spread any further.
Susan Morée: So if you're driving around in your vehicle and you've got a fly in the vehicle, maybe you want to kill it?
Nick Seibel: I mean, I usually want to do that anyway. One of the things they said is you can't really tell, and it doesn't really look any different from any other fly, to the naked eye.
Susan Morée: I don't think I'm going to get too close to a fly anyway to examine it.
Nick Seibel: This is where having a newspaper subscription really comes in handy because that rolled up newspaper is excellent.
Nick Seibel: That's right.
Susan Morée: I love that you got a little plug in there. And let's talk about the candidate forums for District 39. The election is in November. What was your forum like?
Nick Seibel: Yeah, well, early voting got started, well, got started yesterday, in fact, across New Mexico. Not a lot of contested races on the local level here in Grant County. Most of it was decided in the primary. But there is of course a contested race for Grant County Sheriff, but the Republican candidate there declined to participate, so we won't be able to have one there, which left us with New Mexico House District 39, which is currently held by Republican Luis Terrazas. He's being opposed by Democrat Raul Turrieta, and they squared off in a forum last Friday night sponsored by the Daily Press. That was just one night after they met in a similar forum sponsored by the Grant County Beat, which is an online publication here. In the Thursday night forum, the Beat forum, was confrontational, a little testy at times. And things started out that way in the Friday forum, too. They definitely, you know, the candidates took some hot shots at each other. But it definitely ended on an odd note. I mean, having done a lot of these candidate forums, I can't ever recall anything quite like that. The last audience question that we asked was about, asking each one of them to say something positive about the other's service to the community. And it really got emotional. In fact, the candidates at the conclusion of the question stood up and hugged it out, which was the main photo on our front page on Tuesday at the Daily Press.
Susan Morée: Let's move on to Gila Regional Medical Center. You've got some news for us about that.
Nick Seibel: Yeah, and that's pretty positive news there. Gila Regional, of course, is the county-owned hospital here in Silver City. And they've been named a regional hub in the new state health initiative known as the Healthy Horizons Initiative. They're gonna be coordinating the expenditure of about a little more than $15 million to improve rural healthcare in this part of the state. So Gila Regional is right at the center of that.
Susan Morée: Okay, and where can readers find these stories, Nick?
Nick Seibel: Check us out anytime online at scdailypress.com.

articles.title_orig: Nobel chemistry prize goes to pair who solved mystery of 'mirror image' molecules
articles.title_zh: Nobel chemistry prize goes to pair who solved mystery of 'mirror image' molecules
articles.content_orig:
Henri B Kagan and Kensō Soai awarded prize for discovery that has aided understanding of how medicines work in the body
The Nobel prize in chemistry 2026 has been awarded to two scientists for discoveries that showed how chemical reactions can produce an overwhelming excess of one of two mirror image forms of a molecule.
Henri B Kagan at Paris-Sud University in France and Kensō Soai at Tokyo University of Science in Japan have been awarded the prize “for the discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, Sweden, on Wednesday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000).
Many molecules, including amino acids that form the building blocks of proteins, can exist in two forms that contain the same atoms, but are mirror images of one another, much like a person’s left and right hands. This property is known as chirality.
However, the chemistry underpinning life is surprisingly “homochiral”, or same-handed. Proteins are built almost exclusively from L-amino acids, while the sugars that form the backbone of DNA and RNA have the opposite D- configuration.
How this homochirality could have emerged when chemical reactions in the laboratory typically produce equal quantities of both forms had long puzzled scientists. The question also had practical consequences: “Although these molecules look very similar, they can behave very differently when they interact with other molecules,” said Prof Andre Cobb, an organic chemist at King’s College London.
“This matters enormously for medicines because many of the molecules in our bodies, including proteins that drugs target, are themselves chiral. So the ‘left-handed’ and ‘right-handed’ versions of a drug can interact with the body in different ways which can lead to different or weakened drug effects.”
The drug thalidomide provides a potent example. During the early 1960s, thousands of children were affected by birth defects after their mothers were prescribed it to combat morning sickness during pregnancy. Researchers subsequently found differences in the biological effects of the drug’s two mirror image forms.
Manufacturers wanted a way of steering reactions towards particular forms of the molecules that they produced, and Kagan and Soai eventually provided a solution.
It began in 1986, when Kagan discovered that a relatively small imbalance between left- and right-handed forms of a catalyst could create a greater excess of one of the mirror image products than the other.
Soai took the idea further, developing a reaction in which the molecules produced themselves acted as catalysts for making more of themselves, a process known as autocatalysis. “You have to be aware, this is probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry ever,” said Prof Peter Somfai, an organic chemist at Lund University and a member of the Nobel committee for chemistry.
In 2003, Soai demonstrated a reaction that produced almost exclusively one mirror-image form, reproducing the kind of molecular one-handedness found in living organisms for the first time.
Speaking by telephone at Wednesday’s announcement, Soai, 76, said he was “very proud” of the experiment as it offered a potential explanation for how the molecular one-handedness of life could have arisen. He described hearing the news about the prize as “one of the most exciting days of my life”.
Taken together, Kagan and Soai’s discoveries had “reshaped our understanding of molecular chirality, how it is created, amplified and transmitted”, Somfai said.
These insights have since become embedded in the development of catalysts that steer chemical reactions towards producing a particular mirror image form across different industries. “It is in the backsides of our heads all the time,” said Somfai.
“It might be difficult to say that this drug or that drug was developed using this. I would say all of them because we use this as a tool. We use this as an understanding of how to develop catalysts and how they function.”

articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lays a wreath during a state memorial ceremony in memory of those killed in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel, at Mount Herzl cemetery in Jerusalem on Oct. 5. Debbie Hill/Pool UPI via AP hide caption
TEL AVIV, Israel — As Israel marks three years since Hamas launched its surprise Oct. 7 attacks, Israelis are reeling from new revelations in Israeli and U.S. media that the country had been repeatedly warned by its regional allies that Hamas was planning to attack.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was personally warned about a potential Hamas attack, and his security agencies were notified repeatedly, in the weeks and days leading up to Oct. 7, 2023, four people in the Middle East with direct knowledge of the warnings told NPR.
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz , The New York Times and The Atlantic first reported about the warnings.
Netanyahu has denied he was warned, calling the reports "fake news" and filing a defamation lawsuit last week against Israeli news outlets that published them. He and his defense minister have issued new warnings that Hamas could try to attack or "challenge" Israel on this Oct. 7 memorial day and leading up to national elections later this month.
But the Oct. 7, 2023, security failure — as well as Netanyahu's repeated refusal to take responsibility for it — has become a lightning rod in Israel as the prime minister seeks a new term in national elections this month.
"You didn't protect my son," yelled out one bereaved Israeli father whose son was killed in the Hamas-led attack, as the prime minister spoke at a memorial ceremony this week for the victims.
One warning came directly from the leader of Hamas in Gaza weeks before Oct. 7, a Palestinian mediator told NPR and other media outlets.
Former Palestinian Authority official Sufian Abu Zaida said he helped mediate secret Hamas-Israel talks for more than a year leading up to Oct. 7. He said Hamas wanted Israel to release Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and offered in exchange to release two living Israeli hostages and the bodies of two Israeli soldiers held in Gaza for years. But he said Israel was unwilling to release as many prisoners as Hamas had demanded.
On Sept. 14, 2023, Abu Zaida said, Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar dictated a message for him to deliver to Israel: "By the end of September, we will put cards on the table. There will be an earthquake in the negotiations, and the Israelis should prepare to empty their prisons."
He did not know what kind of earthquake Sinwar meant, but he said he sent the message to an Israeli intelligence official who acknowledged receiving it and to Mohammed Dahlan, a Palestinian confidant of the leader of the United Arab Emirates.
"What happened [on] the 7th of October is needless," Abu Zaida told NPR.
Days before the Oct. 7 attacks, the leader of the United Arab Emirates, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, called Netanyahu and told him that Hamas' leader in Gaza was planning a big assault against Israel, according to a person close to Dahlan. Dahlan was the Palestinian Authority's head of security in Gaza before Hamas seized control of the territory in 2007.
The Emirati leader told Netanyahu in a phone call that lasted more than 40 minutes that a "quake" would hit the region if no progress was achieved regarding a prisoner deal between Hamas and Israel, the person said.
The person spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity because of the diplomatic sensitivity of the call. The phone call was previously reported by Haaretz and The New York Times .
The UAE did not deny the report, saying only that it maintained dialogue with Israel.
People visit a memorial at a police station attacked by Hamas on Oct. 7, 2023, three years prior, in Sderot, southern Israel, on Oct. 4. Oded Balilty/AP hide caption
A senior Egyptian official told NPR that Egypt had specific intelligence about Hamas movements and that Egypt's head of intelligence at the time, Abbas Kamel, had traveled to Israel with two other senior officials and met with Israel's Mossad and Shin Bet intelligence chiefs.
The official said Kamel relayed a warning that Gaza was on the verge of an "explosion" because of Israel's blockade, the condition of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and concerns that Israel might move to annex the occupied West Bank.
The official was not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. The Atlantic reported that Kamel's visit to Israel was on Sept 26.
Nimrod Novik, a fellow at the Israel Policy Forum think tank and a former top adviser to late Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres, told NPR that he was informed before Oct. 7 by a person with firsthand knowledge that Egypt had delivered warnings to several senior Israeli officials that "Gaza is about to explode in your face."
Novik said one warning was an "urgent and dramatic message" from Egypt, delivered to a person close to Netanyahu some 10 days prior to Oct. 7.
"I'm certain that the issue of the early warnings on October 7 is going to continue to play with heightened emotions as we approach Election Day," said Novik. "This is going to be an indictment for history, not just for the elections."
Netanyahu has blamed Israeli security organizations for failing to stop the Oct. 7 attacks. He and his government have yet to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the failures around Oct. 7, despite public demand.
The new reports about warnings issued to Israel "actually turn the story on its head," pointing the finger right back at the prime minister, said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
"It violates the basic narrative that Netanyahu tries to tell Israelis," said Talshir.
NPR's Aya Batrawy contributed to this report.

Built on the world's largest live video map, Atlas turns authentic video into real-world intelligence for AI, search and commerce.
SAN FRANCISCO , Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Atmosfy today announced Atlas, a platform that gives AI a live view of the physical world. Atlas is built on Atmosfy , the world's largest live video map, with more than 500 million experiences spanning 100 million places across 20,000 cities in 150 countries.
The video map is powered by Atmosfy's global community, capturing moments at restaurants, bars, hotels, stadiums and other places around the world. Each video connects a real place to a moment in time.
Spectra, Atlas's latest intelligence model, turns those videos into time capsules, connecting them into a single, living picture of the world.
Building on existing partnerships with Capital One, Expedia, SeatGeek, GetYourGuide, Virgin Hotels, Resy, Funko and others, Atmosfy is expanding through Atlas into video and data licensing for frontier AI models.
"As AI takes on more decisions for people, it needs to understand what's happening in the real world," said Michael Ebel, Founder and CEO of Atmosfy. "Where to go, what to book, what to recommend: those decisions depend on how places and experiences are changing. Atlas gives AI a continuously updated view of that world."
Atmosfy is the "what's happening" app for millennials and Gen Z. Its global community maps what's happening across 20,000 cities through real-world video, creating city-based feeds that show where people are going and what they're doing right now.
Atmosfy is backed by Redpoint Ventures, Capital One Ventures, Canaan Partners, Industry Ventures, Streamlined Ventures, DNX Ventures, Suntory Ventures, Plug and Play, and others. See Atlas in action at atmosfy.io .
