articles.title_orig: World Athletics referee and race walking judge Costin's steps to success
articles.title_zh: World Athletics referee and race walking judge Costin's steps to success
articles.content_orig:
Zuzana Costin at the World Athletics U20 Championships Oregon 26 ( © World Athletics Media Academy Lenny Patram Jr. )
Zuzana Costin is a former athlete turned official, currently the only active female technical official in the world to hold both World Athletics Gold Level Referee and Gold Level Race Walking Judge qualifications.
The two-time Olympian, who competed in the 20km race walk at the Athens 2004 and Beijing 2008 Games, most recently served as a race walking judge and referee during the World Athletics U20 Championships Oregon 26. While there, she reflected on her journey in athletics.
You hold both World Athletics Gold Level Referee and Gold Level Race Walking Judge qualifications – currently the only active female technical official in the world to do so. What does this achievement mean to you?
"There are three of us who hold both qualifications but, yes, I am the only female official. It’s quite amazing to have achieved this. I always try to do the best that I can, therefore it’s nice to see that the work I have put in was recognised, and it paid off."
When you first began your journey as a technical official, did you ever imagine you would reach this level?
"No, I didn’t. I got involved in athletics at a very young age. My dad (Jozef Malik) was the Vice President of the federation (Slovak Athletic Federation) for several years and was active as an administrator, coach and also as an official, so I grew up in the world of athletics. Any time he organised any competitions, I was helping out. So it has always been a part of my life and I never thought about it too much at that stage. Achieving this level in officiating in athletics after finishing my racing career gives me a strong sense of accomplishment and satisfaction."
Throughout your career, have there been mentors who helped shape your journey?
"Undeniably, my dad played a big role at the beginning of my journey and he has kept supporting me since.
"After retiring from being an athlete, I started to officiate in Ireland on a regular basis (I had moved there a few years beforehand). I met with support and encouragement to pursue this to an international level. I was very lucky that I was immersed in an environment where people knew what they were doing, not just on a local level but on an international one, too. So, whenever I came across any problems, I had people I could rely on.
"After passing the Silver level exam, I started getting appointments at European competitions and there were always senior technical officials who were happy to share their knowledge and experience with ‘newbies’.
"That was also the case during one of my first big international appointments as a member of the Jury of Appeal at the European Championships in Berlin where Anna Riccardi was our chief. She took me under her wing, gave me confidence and guided me through this new experience.
"During the Covid-19 pandemic, European Athletics began organising online webinars for technical officials, focusing heavily on the practical aspects of officiating. Those webinars were primary led by Chris Cohen and Niels van der Aar and they helped me to become a more knowledgeable and effective official.
"Later, I was selected for the European Athletics mentoring programme for technical delegates and was appointed as a mentee technical delegate for the European Championships in Rome. I was fortunate to have Chris and Niels as my mentors; their guidance provided invaluable insights and allowed me to expand my knowledge even further."
What practical support is most beneficial for upcoming female officials during the early stages of their careers?
"Having someone you can turn to, talk to and learn from is major. Mentorship is something you can’t replace, especially when you are trying to excel.
"After World Athletics changed its educational programme for officials to the current one, it really opened the door for younger people. Originally, the educational programme and exams to become an international official were only in English, which could be a bit of a barrier for people who don’t have a good standard of English. That is still the case for the Gold level. And this could be something that a mentor could help with – dismantling the language barrier. However, for the lower levels, World Athletics has gradually introduced more languages in which its certification courses and exams can be taken. This shift definitely benefits new candidates who don’t have a sufficient command of English."
Since you started your career, have you seen an increase in more female judges, applicants or volunteers for athletics?
"Absolutely. I don’t remember seeing many female officials in the leading positions when I started, and that has definitely changed now. Also, World Athletics’ encouragement to member federations to enter an equal number of female and male candidates for exams has started to pay off. Panels of international officials are now nearly gender balanced.
"I have also seen a growth in the numbers of younger officials, with more opportunities and positions available for them. It’s more achievable and something that one can work towards now."
What kind of advice would you give someone, especially a younger woman, who is interested in following your footsteps or becoming a judge in athletics?
"Now is the right time. Ask your federation about upcoming courses and exams. If you get opportunities to take part in them or you get any appointments, don’t turn them down because you can always learn something. You might not succeed all the time, but you learn from the experience.
"It is also important to believe in yourself and to have someone, or a group of people, that you can get support from.
"It is nice to see new candidates growing in confidence. When they first get started, it’s all very nerve-racking and there’s so much going on all at once – it creates a lot of feelings of fear. But that’s a normal thing to experience. Sometimes all they need is someone in their corner telling them that this is normal, to believe in themselves, and that someone else has confidence in them."
What kind of legacy do you hope to leave – not only through the competitions you’ve officiated, but through the people you’ve inspired?
"I just hope that all the younger officials coming in see that they can do this. That this, as well as whatever else they want to strive for, is achievable regardless of whether they are coming from a country with a strong tradition of international officiating or not. And that the journey of being an international official can start at any age."
Ash Wehrly for the World Athletics Media Academy
Launched in March, the World Athletics pledge initiative forms part of the organisation’s contribution to the International Women’s Day 2026 global campaign, #GiveToGain, which calls on individuals and organisations to give their time, resources and support to help forge gender equality through abundant giving. By encouraging stakeholders to pledge mentoring hours, World Athletics is turning the #GiveToGain message into practical action across the sport. Learn more on the Women in Athletics website .

The four astronauts of SpaceX’s Crew-12 mission are heading home after nearly 10 months in space.
Crew-12 's Crew Dragon capsule, named "Freedom," undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) on Wednesday (Oct. 7) at 8:05 a.m. EDT (1205 GMT). If all goes according to plan, Freedom will splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Thursday (Oct. 8) at 11:34 a.m. EDT (1534 GMT).
Return-to-Earth coverage will begin on Thursday at 10:20 a.m. EDT (1420 GMT). Freedom will conduct its deorbit burn around 10:46 a.m. EDT (1446 GMT), then splash down in the Pacific at 11:34 a.m. EDT (1534 GMT). You can watch that coverage here when the time comes, courtesy of NASA.
Then, at 1:15 p.m. EDT (1715 GMT) on Thursday, NASA and SpaceX will hold a press conference to discuss Crew-12's homecoming and the launch of the company's robotic CRS-35 cargo mission to the ISS, which is targeted for Oct. 13. Participants in the briefing are:
The Crew-12 astronauts are Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway of NASA, ESA's Sophie Adenot, and Andrey Fedyaev of the Russian space agency Roscosmos . Meir and Fedyaev had each been to space once before, while Crew-12 was the first mission for Hathaway and Adenot.
The quartet launched to the ISS atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on Feb. 13 . Their arrival brought the station up to its normal complement of seven crewmembers. It had been operating with a skeleton crew of three since Jan. 15, when SpaceX's Crew-11 mission headed home a month early to deal with a medical issue experienced by one of its astronauts, NASA's Mike Fincke .
That was the first medical evacuation in the long history of the ISS. But it was not an emergency situation, NASA officials stressed at the time, and Fincke is doing fine now here on terra firma. (He retired in August with a total of 549 days in space, the fourth-most ever for a NASA astronaut.)
Crew-12, in turn, has been relieved by the four-person Crew-13 , which arrived at the ISS on Thursday (Oct. 1). Crew-13 made it to the station less than eight hours after launch — the quickest-ever ISS trip for an American spacecraft. (The world record is just over three hours , by a Russian Soyuz crewed vehicle.)
Crew-13 was originally supposed to launch on Sept. 12. However, an issue with the propulsion system on its Crew Dragon capsule, named "Grace," pushed things back, giving Crew-12 a few extra weeks in orbit.
The Crew-12 astronauts were very busy during their nearly 10 months off Earth, performing a variety of maintenance work and dozens of scientific experiments.
Then there were the spacewalks . Meir performed four of them, bringing her lifetime total to seven. And on Aug. 18, Adenot stepped outside the ISS, becoming the first French woman ever to walk in space. She did two more over the next two weeks, including one with Meir, which was just the sixth all-female extravehicular activity in the station's history.
The Crew-12 astronauts are doubtless feeling a mix of emotions about their homecoming, as big transitions are always bittersweet. Indeed, Meir gave us a sense of this a few weeks back.
"What I'm looking forward to most is seeing my three-and-a-half-year-old daughter,” Meir said during a Sept. 16 call with reporters from the station.
"I'm so looking forward to seeing nature again," she added, "feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves, experiencing all those things that we don't have up here. But I will very, very much miss being weightless all the time and the incredible views that we have."
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. articles.title_orig: Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
articles.title_zh: Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
articles.content_orig:
For scientists searching for life beyond Earth, rocky planets with atmospheres are among the most promising places to investigate. An atmosphere is essential for maintaining liquid water on a planet's surface. Yet among the more than 6,300 exoplanets cataloged thus far, most are not rocky, and only a small number of known rocky planets appear to possess atmospheres.
Now, researchers have added another world to that short list. In a study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , a team led by University of Chicago scientist Brandon Park Coy reports evidence of an atmosphere surrounding HD 3167 b, a rocky super-Earth located 154 light-years away in the constellation Pisces. The intensely hot planet, classified as a "lava world," completes an orbit around its star in only one Earth day.
"What's so surprising is that the closer a rocky planet orbits its star, the harder it should be to have an atmosphere, because it's bombarded by stellar wind and gets more high-energy photons from the star. But it seems that many of these lava worlds do," explained Edwin Kite, UChicago associate professor of geophysical sciences and co-author of the study. "These planets are too hot for life, but by studying them, we can say something about the processes that matter for other rocky worlds."
In the Q&A below,Coy, a graduate student in Kite's group and first author on the study, explains why atmospheres on lava worlds are scientifically valuable, how researchers detected evidence for this one, and what they hope to learn next.
What was the goal of the survey that found this atmosphere-bearing exoplanet?
One of the driving questions that the James Webb Space Telescope is being used to answer is whether planets orbiting stars much smaller than the sun have atmospheres. It appears that most of those terrestrial planets don't -- they're just bare rock.
But surprisingly, we've found evidence that the majority of lava worlds -- similar in composition to Earth and Venus but much, much hotter -- might have atmospheres. Five terrestrial planets found with atmospheres, including the one described in this study, have been ultra-hot.
This planet, however, is the coldest lava world found so far with evidence of an atmosphere. This is interesting because we're trying to understand the temperature transition between planets with and without atmospheres.
The result is the first from a program led by Megan Weiner Mansfield, PhD'21, who's now at the University of Maryland. The goal of the program, which is looking at 10 ultra-hot lava worlds, is to see if there's a critical temperature over which you start seeing planets with atmospheres.
"We're interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world." -- Study author Brandon Park Coy
How can you tell if an exoplanet has an atmosphere?
Right now, directly looking at Earth-like planets for signs of life is out of reach. Instead, we can use the Webb telescope to detect light in the mid-infrared wavelength range to estimate the temperature of exoplanets, which can tell us if they might have atmospheres.
There are two primary ways that we study exoplanets. One is called transit, when the planet goes in front of the host star. Another called secondary eclipse, which is the method we used for this study, is when the planet passes behind its star, and we can measure how much light is lost. That difference tells us how much mid-infrared light comes from the planet itself, which essentially tells us how hot the planet is.
If a planet doesn't have an atmosphere, its star-facing, day side should be as hot as theoretically possible based on how reflective its surface is and its distance from the star. But an atmosphere would help redistribute heat from the day side to the night side. We see this happen on Venus -- there's almost no difference in surface temperature between the day and night sides, or between the poles and the equator. If a planet has an atmosphere, it might also have clouds that reflect incoming starlight and cool the dayside. So if a planet's day side is cooler than the maximum possible, it likely has an atmosphere.
The subject of this study, HD 3167 b, is noticeably cooler than its expected maximum, providing strong evidence that it has an atmosphere.
What do you think HD 3167 b's atmosphere is made of?
These lava worlds are so-named because the surface facing their star is likely melted rock. We think that HD 3167 b might have a silicate-rich composition, with a similar mixture of minerals that make up Earth's mantle. Before this study, we expected that any atmosphere on these ultra-hot planets would be composed of vaporized rock, but we're starting to see evidence that some might have heavier gases like carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, or water in their atmospheres.
The makeup of HD 3167 b's atmosphere is still up in the air. That's one reason we're so interested in getting new observations.
Why is this result important?
Because the four other lava worlds found to have atmospheres are in the ultra-hot regime, it raises questions about whether there's a critical transition temperature when silicate atmospheres start becoming very thick. Is there a temperature where these planets form silicate cloud decks that might reflect incoming radiation to space and cool its day side? This relatively cooler planet helps us better characterize and nail down this transition.
Despite how inhospitable they are for life, we're also interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world. We think that very early in the solar system's history, when the terrestrial planets formed, they were extremely hot due to the energy from all of the planetesimal collisions. Earth had what's known as a magma ocean stage with an entirely liquid surface. This result gives us a window into studying what conditions may have been like in Earth's first couple of million years.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Two weeks ago, journalists in the San Francisco Bay Area got to try two hot new wearables that weigh only around 100 grams: the just-revealed Meta VR Glasses , and the long-awaited transparent Google XR glasses built in partnership with Xreal. It turns out they’re going head-to-head. Xreal has just opened Aura pre-orders starting at $1,279 , $20 less than the Meta VR Glasses.
That’s for the Xreal Aura with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage; there’ll also be a 16GB / 512GB config for $1,499. (Xreal couldn’t tell us whether the 16GB of RAM would be important for some apps by publish time.)
Both the Google / Xreal Aura and Meta’s VR Glasses let you overlay virtual objects and desktops on the real world. Both are relatively lightweight because they’ve got a cord — their Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite chips and batteries both live in a compute puck, which runs either Meta’s Horizon OS or Android XR. Both greet you with a grid of floating app icons to choose from.
But they’re very different experiences in practice, primarily because the Google / Xreal Aura has transparent lenses, while the Meta VR Glasses use passthrough vision to let you see the real world and offers more immersion. While the Xreal Aura has one of the largest transparent fields of view yet at 70 degrees diagonal, it’s still smaller than Meta’s passthrough glasses. I wrote all about it in this story , and it’s just one of many differences.
The Meta VR Glasses also have eye tracking, like the Apple Vision Pro, so you can select things just by looking at them and pinching fingers resting on your lap; the Google / Xreal Aura has a touchpad built into the compute puck and hand-tracking to give you virtual laser pointers. (Both let you connect to other peripherals and display other devices too — and you can plug devices with USB-C DisplayPort video right in.)
And, of course, you’ve got your Android apps inside the Xreal Aura, or your Quest games inside the VR Glasses.
I don’t think any journalist can tell you which is better yet; you may want to wait for reviews. We also have yet to test Android XR extensively: while Samsung and Google did technically ship the $1,799 Galaxy XR with Android XR last year, they didn’t send one to The Verge for review.
The Meta VR Glasses aren’t due until spring 2027, but Xreal isn’t necessarily shipping lots of pairs before then. Today, the only people who can preorder the Xreal glasses are those who already put in a reservation , and only the first 2,000 “Founder’s Edition” pairs are necessarily coming at “launch.” Those will ship this year, Xreal CEO and co-founder Chi Xu tells The Verge .
It might not take till the end of the year. Xreal’s press release does say they “will begin shipping soon” and that the “launch” is “now just weeks away,” but those are wiggly, and again, those timeframes are just for early adopters. If you don’t have a preorder, “Orders will open to the general public in the coming weeks.” The glasses will also only ship in the US, Canada, Japan, and South Korea to start, before expanding to other regions in 2027.
I’m already a fan of Xreal’s older glasses and how they let me watch my 3D movies with a 57-degree field of view, and I’m intrigued by the puck. I’d love to see how much more useful these glasses are with the new 70-degree view.

articles.title_zh: Collisions between dipolar molecules ‘switch off’ at low energies
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for registering with Physics World If you'd like to change your details at any time, please visit My account
Researchers in the Netherlands have shown that they can turn off the dipole moment of molecules that are normally polar, drastically altering the molecules’ behaviour in low-energy collisions. The discovery – which was only possible after the team cleared a major experimental hurdle – has implications for ultracold chemistry and could also lead to a better understanding of polarity, with benefits for quantum simulation and computation.
Chemical reactions are full of complexity and chaos, making them hard to study at the atomic and molecular level. Before attempting to do so, scientists typically cool the reactants to just above absolute zero, which restricts their movement and vibrations. Despite these restrictions, however, interactions between ultracold molecules remain poorly understood, especially when the molecules have an electric dipole moment.
In 2023 experimental physicist Bas van de Meerakker and theorist colleagues at the Radboud University Nijmegen in the Netherlands shone a ray of light on this murky area by studying the collision cross-section (that is, the likelihood that collisions will take place) between molecules of ammonia (NH 3 ) at low energies. Their simulations showed that this cross-section falls off sharply as the energy decreases. This contradicts the classical picture of polarity, which suggests that the cross-section should continuously increase.
The Radboud team explained this discrepancy by noting that in the classical picture, polar molecules such as ammonia have a permanently asymmetric charge distribution – a dipole moment – due to the arrangement of the bonds between their constituent atoms. The quantum mechanical picture, in contrast, depicts an isolated molecule in a specific quantum state as having a definite parity, or symmetry. Because of this symmetry, the molecule’s net dipole moment in the lab frame is exactly zero.
According to this quantum picture, collisions between polar molecules at high speeds (high energies) cause these opposite parity states to mix via interactions between the molecules’ electrostatic fields. In the process, they essentially “turn on” each other’s dipole moments, causing them to attract each other and increasing the collision cross-section. At low speeds, however, the molecules cannot get close enough to trigger this mutual mixing. As a result, their dipole moments effectively switch off, and their collision rates drop drastically.
The Radboud team’s next step was to prove experimentally that this is indeed what happens. However, colliding cold molecules generally requires using electric fields to merge two molecular beams. When molecules in the two beams have very similar dipole moments, this is very difficult, because using an electric field to steer one beam automatically affects the path of the other. The risk is that the beams never overlap at all.
To overcome this obstacle, van de Meerakker and colleagues combined a 2.6 m Stark decelerator, a curved hexapole guide and a merged quadrupole/hexapole trap into a device that can overlap the beams at just the right position, with minimal angle between them. In this way, they achieved sufficient overlap to observe low-energy collisions. They then experimentally verified the predicted energy-dependent changes in cross-section for NH 3 -NH 3 collisions, while also showing that this dependence is different when they replace hydrogen atoms with deuterium (NH 3 -ND 3 or ND 3 -ND 3 collisions).
According to van de Meerakker, the fact that cross sections drop at low energies could make it hard to perform experiments that require scattering to take place in crossed or merged beams. On the other hand, experiments in which dipolar molecules are stored in traps could benefit, as lower inelastic cross-sections mean fewer molecules are lost from the trap.
As for future work, van de Meerakker says the team plans to add a controlled electric field to the beam overlap region. The mechanism they discovered is expected to respond extremely sensitively to this field, with even small electric fields changing cross sections by orders of magnitude and thereby providing a “knob” with which to control collision outcomes. “It was exactly this type of control that sparked our interest in cold and ultracold molecules two decades ago, and it is very exciting that this is now within reach in our scattering experiments,” van de Meerakker tells Physics World .
Quantum superchemistry emerges in the laboratory
Tim Langen , a physicist at Austria’s Vienna University of Technology who was not involved in this research, describes it as important because it provides experimental evidence for a phenomenon that had mainly been discussed theoretically. In his view, the results support the idea that effective dipolar interactions become strongly suppressed at low collision energies. He also finds the experimental approach “impressive” as it enables measurements in a regime that was previously difficult to access. “Overall, I find the work convincing and expect it to be of broad interest to researchers working on cold and ultracold molecules,” Langen concludes.
The research is published in Nature Chemistry .

articles.title_orig: The Morning Risk Report: Hackers Use Chinese AI Tool to Hit South Korean Banks, Exposing New Risk
articles.title_zh: The Morning Risk Report: Hackers Use Chinese AI Tool to Hit South Korean Banks, Exposing New Risk
articles.content_orig:
President Lee Jae Myung directed officials to investigate after cyberattacks hit Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank, and others
JEON HEON-KYUN / Getty Images
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung warned Tuesday that AI models appear to have been used in a series of cyberattacks against the country's banks, directing officials to investigate breaches that exposed personal data belonging to 68,000 customers across seven financial institutions.
"In some hacking incidents, signs have emerged of AI being used, causing considerable public concern and anxiety," Lee said during a cabinet meeting. "Please establish the circumstances swiftly and clearly, and concentrate personnel and resources on minimizing the damage."
South Korea's National Police Agency announced it had begun a comprehensive inquiry into the attacks, according to NBC News . Investigators believe the breaches involved Artex AI, an open-source penetration-testing tool built by Chinese cybersecurity engineer Li Puhua — known by the alias Autumn — that uses AI agents to automate vulnerability discovery and attack planning. Artex draws on external AI models including Anthropic's Opus, OpenAI's GPT, and DeepSeek to carry out its operations with limited human input.
Shinhan Bank and KB Kookmin Bank were among the confirmed targets, the Financial Services Commission said . Hana Bank and Woori Bank also suffered breaches, according to Reuters . Shinhan Bank's breach affected 25,000 customers, while Kookmin Bank saw credit card data for 119,000 clients exposed, according to BleepingComputer . Authorities have not yet disclosed the full scale of the breaches or identified perpetrators.
The Financial Supervisory Service and the Financial Security Institute provided the financial sector with information on 28 IP addresses tied to the intrusions, along with associated country data, according to Reuters. Authorities said the attacks originated from addresses across roughly a dozen countries, including the U.S., Japan, and Germany, and said they were seeking international cooperation.
The Financial Services Commission convened an emergency meeting on Oct. 2 and issued a set of directives to financial firms, requiring them to audit internet-facing systems, tighten access controls and authentication requirements, limit unnecessary data exposure, and coordinate threat intelligence sharing industrywide.
Mun Chong-hyun, head of the Genians Security Center, wrote on LinkedIn that a number of analysts in the threat intelligence community have concluded the intrusions relied on AI-driven attack automation, according to BleepingComputer. "Cybersecurity attacks powered by AI agents have been increasing in South Korea, and I expect they will grow in number worldwide in the future," Mun said.
The South Korean attacks fit a broader pattern of AI-enabled intrusions in 2026. A Chinese-speaking hacker used AI agents to breach up to 100 companies within a five-day window last month, stealing more than 600,000 credit card records for a total outlay of around $8,000. South Korean cybersecurity stocks jumped as much as 30% on Tuesday.

Quiles heads to Indonesia for his next chance at match point, but what does the #28 need to do to clinch the title?
It’s a big weekend for Maximo Quiles (CFMOTO Gaviota Aspar Team), who has another opportunity to be crowned Champion this weekend. Quiles enters the weekend with a 127-point advantage over his rivals, and with just 125 points remaining up for grabs after Indonesia, the #28 is now faced with another opportunity to be crowned Moto3 World Champion.
Simply put, if Quiles leaves Indonesia with at least a 125-point advantage, then he will be crowned 2026 Moto3 World Champion. Four riders remain in mathematical contention, with Quiles, Alvaro Carpe (Red Bull KTM Ajo), David Almansa (Liqui Moly Dynavolt Intact GP) and Brian Uriarte (Red Bull KTM Ajo) all facing a pivotal weekend.
Ultimately, Quiles has the opportunity to control his own destiny. A victory would crown him World Champion regardless of other results, whilst P2 would also be enough if Almansa finishes P3 or lower. Meanwhile, a third-place finish will secure Quiles the title if Almansa were to finish P4 or below on Sunday.
Finishing outside the podium positions brings Carpe into contention. If Quiles finishes fourth, Carpe would need to score P2 or worse, while Almansa would need to finish P5 or lower. Anything outside of the top five (P6 or lower) for Quiles brings Uriarte back into the picture, increasing the complications.
It has already been an incredible season for Quiles, who has earned nine race wins and 14 podiums from the opening 16 rounds. The #28 has already scored 52 points more than his entire 2025 campaign, underlining just how impressive his form has been this year.

articles.title_orig: Bigger than Manhattan: The record-breaking airport megahub that conquered the world
articles.title_zh: Bigger than Manhattan: The record-breaking airport megahub that conquered the world
articles.content_orig:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This CNN Travel series is, or was, sponsored by the country it highlights. CNN retains full editorial control over subject matter, reporting and frequency of the articles and videos within the sponsorship, in compliance with our policy .
Standing at the crossroad of continents, Istanbul has long been a global linchpin.
As Byzantium and then Constantinople, it controlled trade routes along the Silk Road and maritime passage from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean.
In the golden age of railways, Istanbul was the end point of the Orient Express, at the very cusp of Europe and Asia.
Now, in the 21st century, iGA Istanbul Airport is ruling the skies, having just overtaken London Heathrow as the best-connected airport on the planet.
“They’ve finally got the number one position,” says John Grant, chief analyst at OAG, a global travel data provider which has just released its Megahubs 2026 Index, comparing the world’s top airports.
The rankings are generated by comparing the number of scheduled connections to and from international flights , with the number of destinations served from the airport. They do this through a snapshot look at the busiest day of the year, which this year was August 2.
Gaining the top spot is “an important achievement for iGA Istanbul Airport and reflects the position we have built as a global aviation hub,” airport CEO Selahattin Bilgen tells CNN. “Today, we already serve approximately 350 destinations around the world, with significant room to grow further.”
Amsterdam Airport Schiphol is third place in this year’s ranking, followed by Kuala Lumpur at No.4 and Chicago O’Hare at No.5.
It’s been a swift and impressive rise for the award-winning $12 billion Istanbul Airport, which opened to much fanfare in 2018, about 20 miles outside Istanbul on the European side. This is a hub built for scale: Its huge 1.4-million-square-meter terminal is the world’s largest under one roof and the whole 76.5-million-square-meter site is bigger than Manhattan.
More than 84 million passengers pass through each year, making it the eighth busiest airport in the world. However, the long-term plan is to increase capacity to 200 million passengers per year, which is double the annual number currently handled by Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta, the world’s busiest airport.
“They’re going to be unassailable in the coming years,” says Grant. “They’ve got runway capacity. They’ve got a national airline that is hugely successful and continues to grow with new fleet orders. They’re very close to some of the most emergent markets in the world, such as Central Asia. They’ve benefited partly from the Middle East situation. They’re just very well placed.”
Istanbul Airport opened its fourth main runway last month and the end goal is for the hub to have nine: six main and three reserve.
The new  2,820-meter-long runway is its first to run east to west, meaning a reduction in taxiing and airborne times for westbound aircraft, saving time and fuel.
“They’re the only airport in the world that is licensed for three simultaneous runway operations,” says Grant, “You can build more frequency at those peak hours, and it gives you more operational flexibility. If you’ve got three runways, then you’re likely to improve your punctuality.”
Secrets of the sultan’s palace where concubines and eunuchs lived
Turkish Airlines has an 80% share of flights at Istanbul Airport and plays a key role in the hub’s success. Two years ago, it entered Guinness World Records for its achievement in flying to more countries than any other airline: 130 in total, as of 2026.
It operates a modern and rapidly expanding fleet of more than 500 Boeing and Airbus aircraft, including a diverse mix of narrow and widebody planes.
A younger fleet makes “a better impression” on customers, says Viktoriia Myroniuk, a senior lecturer in air transport management at the UK’s Cranfield University, reflecting on the polished service that helped earn Turkish Airlines its recent Skytrax award for Best Airline in Europe .
Newer aircraft are also more efficient, which, in this time of rising fuel prices, gives the airline a competitive edge, allowing them to lower ticket prices.
Selahattin Bilgen, CEO of iGA Istanbul Airport, tells CNN, “The efficiency and cost advantages we provide continue to attract new airlines to our network each year, and today we are one of only two major hubs worldwide serving the largest number of airlines.”
Infrastructure is equally key to that connectivity. “As a relatively new airport, iGA İstanbul Airport was designed from the outset with growth in mind, providing the capacity and flexibility to accommodate increasing passenger demand and support our role as a major international transfer hub.”
OAG’s 2026 Megahub rankings are inevitably affected by the ongoing disruption in the Middle East, as well as the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
While other airports and regions have suffered, Istanbul Airport and Turkey’s geographical position and diplomatic relations have by chance granted it better fortune.
Istanbul Airport has the flexibility and capacity for growth that its competitors in the region lack. London Heathrow’s plan for a third runway remains highly controversial, due to the environmental impact in a highly built-up corner of southeast England. Amsterdam Schiphol, the world’s third best connected, has a flight cap of 488,000 movements a year.
“The fact that Istanbul Airport is slightly on the outskirts” means “they can operate 24/7,” says Myroniuk.
She also praises Turkish Airlines’ stopover program , which allows connecting passengers to take a break to explore Istanbul and enjoy free accommodation in partner hotels.
“I’m one of those unlucky passengers who really can’t sleep on board” and struggle on economy flights, Myroniuk says, but “your luggage stays with Turkish Airlines. You go to the perfect night’s rest.”
She married her brother, then he died. The monument to her grief was a Wonder of the Ancient World
It’s a form of sustainable tourism, she says, allowing travelers to embrace slower travel and to connect with local culture, rather than notching up cheap connecting flights with no experiences to show for it.
For many passengers it is also easier to get a visa to stop off in Turkey than it would be to take an exploratory tour from an EU airport, so that’s another advantage Istanbul Airport enjoys.
Although it’s hard to make any predictions in these turbulent times, Grant says that “all things being equal,” Istanbul will continue to hold onto its position in 2027.
“I think we’re going to see over the next three or four years the Chinese airports strengthen in their positions. We’re seeing more international growth from Chinese airlines, and that will help them,” he says.
International airlines including British Airways have yet to resume flying to the Middle East, but airports in the region will hopefully “get back to where they were,” says Grant. “All of which will continue to chip away at the position at Heathrow and Amsterdam Schiphol, and Paris, where we have European airports” that are reaching capacity.

articles.title_orig: US Mortgage Rates Jump to 7.49%, Highest Since 2023
articles.title_zh: US Mortgage Rates Jump to 7.49%, Highest Since 2023
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home more challenging at a time when housing prices are already high. Nam Y. Huh/AP hide caption
Carrie Goldstein's dream for a new home started with a family reunion at her cousin's home in Milwaukee. The home was old with character and she could walk anywhere from the front door.
"We were kind of in awe and drooling over her walkability," Goldstein says.
It was the lifestyle Goldstein wanted but lacked in her Cleveland suburb, which she says is also pretty walkable – with one major issue.
"There are lots of sidewalks," she says. "But you can't really go anywhere."
She brainstormed with her husband and realized nearby Rocky River was where they wanted to live. It was still a suburb, but with a quaint downtown and the option to walk to Lake Erie.
But as much as she wanted to move, one thing stopped her cold. The mortgage she would have to pay. Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home impossible for many people at a time when housing prices are also sky high.
Goldstein is running into a problem that's affecting many households at a time when people have already been struggling with years of high inflation: The rising cost of borrowing.
Carrie Goldstein stands outside her home on October 4, 2026. Home prices and mortgage rates prevent her from moving. Mike Goldstein hide caption
Bond markets influence all types of borrowing costs across the economy – and as yields have surged to their highest in decades, they've pushed up all kinds of interest rates paid by consumers, from loans for homes to cars and higher education.
And those rates are likely to continue moving up after the Federal Reserve in September raised interest rates for the first time this year – while signaling an additional hike could come this year.
Rate hikes from the Federal Reserve filter through the economy and are meant to slow down consumer and business spending by making people hesitant to take out a more expensive loan to pay for a car or a home – both essential purchases for many people.
"If you need to borrow, boy, it's really not a good time," says John Diamond, senior director of the Center for Tax and Budget Policy at the Baker Institute.
Buying a home is a key example of how households are affected when borrowing costs rise in the economy.
While mortgage rates were falling at the start of this year, they reversed upward after the U.S. war with Iran spooked the bond market by raising worries about inflation. As a result, mortgage rates, which are influenced by the bond markets, have surged this year.
For example, at the current 7.28% level for the average 30-year fixed rate mortgage, a person could end up paying about $900 more a month compared with the 3% pandemic-era rates for a median priced home.
As expected, fewer homeowners are willing or capable of making that financial leap, even if they have long since outgrown their current home. Existing house sales in August were down about 1.2% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors.
It's not just mortgage costs that are making Americans like Goldstein wince.
Alongside her dreams of owning a home in a walkable neighborhood, Goldstein is ready for a new car. Her old one is 11 years old, has 150,000 miles and plenty of quirks. The repair costs are approaching the point where they'll be more than the value of the actual car.
But a four-year loan for a used car is about three percentage points higher compared with the start of 2022, right around when auto loans began to shed their pandemic-era low rates and started climbing up.
"You can't go and get a car for $150 or $180 bucks anymore a month," she says about the car payments she would be facing.
Although so far the Fed has only delivered a modest quarter of a percentage point, it's adding to the higher borrowing costs at a time when households are already dealing with inflation and higher prices for other types of borrowing.
"It's added to higher mortgage payments. Higher student loan payments. Higher prices because of inflation," Diamond says. "That's what makes it really painful."
And that could mean that households could continue to delay any big purchases requiring a loan.
Goldstein is one of them. She says she can afford to wait on the car and house. But eventually she unsubscribed from real estate updates for that walkable suburb.
"It just became more and more disheartening when I did the math," Goldstein says. "It's just not in the cards."

articles.title_orig: Bulgaria ends search for missing crew after drone strike sinks cargo ship
articles.title_zh: Bulgaria ends search for missing crew after drone strike sinks cargo ship
articles.content_orig:
Bulgarian authorities have ended search operations after confirming no survivors were found following a drone strike that sank a ship off the country’s coast.
Drones hit two commercial vessels early on Tuesday as attacks on Black Sea shipping increase amid an intensifying Russia-Ukraine war . One caught fire, and the other sank.
“There is no trace of the sailors,” Rumen Nikolov, the head of the country’s Maritime Search and Rescue Coordination Centre, told reporters on Wednesday.
The search stopped late on Tuesday and would not continue, he added.
Eighteen Turkish and Indian crew members were rescued from the ship that caught fire, but the crew members from the vessel that sank remain missing.
Authorities have not said how many people are missing, but according to the Maritime.bg specialised website, 10 people were on board the ship.
Nikolov said the ⁠incident occurred in a so-called “responsible search and rescue zone” and not in the country’s territorial waters, which extend to 12 nautical miles off the coast.
“What was found from the sunken ship was one overturned boat, three life rafts and debris from the ship’s equipment that was floating on the surface of the sea,” he said.
Asked whether any debris from the drones had been recovered, Nikolov said: “I have no information about drone debris.”
Prime Minister Rumen Radev has described the attack as “absolutely unacceptable”.
European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen has also condemned the incident.
Bulgarian authorities have said they are not yet able to determine the origin of the drones.
A distress beacon signal from the ship that sank was received at 2:54am on Tuesday (23:54 GMT on Monday), while the distress signal from the other ship was received at 3:23am (00:23 GMT), Nikolov said.
Both commercial ships were managed by Turkiye-based companies, according to the Equasis merchant shipping database.
They were hit about 80 nautical miles (150km) east of the Bulgarian coastal town of Byala.
The strikes came a day after another ship caught fire and sank off the Romanian coast on Monday, killing two people. Ukraine blamed Russia for the drone attack.

articles.title_orig: US death row inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
articles.title_zh: US death row inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
articles.content_orig:
US death row inmate Christa Pike is "conscious and speaking" after surviving a failed execution attempt in Tennessee last week, her lawyers say.
Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care while "handcuffed and shackled to the bed" in hospital, her lawyers said in a statement on Tuesday. An anaesthesiologist advising her team told the BBC that Pike was able to communicate in a "basic way" but did not seem to recall the execution attempt.
Pike, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September in Tennessee.
Experts and her legal team say her apparent recovery is unprecedented.
Pike is believed to be the only person to survive a lethal injection. The execution attempt was described immediately afterwards as a "mess" by Slemmer's mother, who had pushed for Pike to be put to death.
After it became clear Pike would not die, she was taken to hospital, where she remained unconscious for days as medical staff cleared her body of the injected chemical.
In their statement on Tuesday, her lawyers said her prognosis remained unclear, but that "at a minimum, we expect a long recovery".
In additional comments made to the BBC, the anaesthesiologist advising her team said Pike had been taken off a ventilator.
"She has some memories of being in the hospital but no memory, I believe, of the execution attempt," Dr Joel Zivot said of the limited communication that had taken place.
Zivot said Pike was able to recall her name and had made an incorrect guess at the date, believing that the month was still September.
In an earlier interview, Zivot said the likelihood of recovering from lethal injection was low. "Most people who get lethal injection die from it," he explained.
There remained many unknowns, he said, including how much of the drug used by the prison authorities, pentobarbital, got into her system.
"I would not, in any way, say at this point that all the big risks are behind her," he said.
Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, said she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike was conscious and speaking.
There had been seven other cases where prisoners survived executions but in those cases, executioners were not able to inject anything into the inmates' veins, Denno told the BBC.
Pike "is the only person for whom some kind of toxin has been injected", she said.
"They did everything they were supposed to do as part of the execution process, and it simply didn't work," Denno said. "This has never happened before."
Speaking to Radio 4's Today programme, a local journalist who witnessed the attempted execution said that he, too, did not know of "an exact precedent".
Steven Hale, a journalist for the Nashville Banner, said the case raised many questions, including "what must this be like for the victim's family, who for 30 years has been told we are gonna give you justice and justice is us executing Christa Pike".
Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong after twice injecting her with the chemical pentobarbital.
Zivot has suggested the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under Pike's skin than to have entered her bloodstream in a quantity that was sufficient to kill her.
Pike's lawyers previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins could scupper the execution and cause her pain.
While the incident is investigated, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state is resigning.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
Shipp was 17 years old at the time, meaning that he was spared the death penalty for his part in the attack because he was not yet legally an adult at the time. He remains in prison.
Pike's lawyers are scheduled to appear in court in Nashville on Wednesday. They also plan to hold a news conference outside the court.
In their latest update, they repeated their call for Lee to use his powers to commute Pike's sentence to the lower punishment of life in prison without parole.
In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which tracks information about such cases.
For lethal injections, such incidents have typically occurred due to difficulty obtaining reliable IV access to the veins, though the underlying reason differs from person to person.
In cases the centre has documented, all failures happened before the lethal  drugs could be administered. The last failed lethal injection that was tracked happened earlier this year - also in Tennessee.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.

articles.title_zh: Real-world VOYAGER data on faricimab in nAMD, DME, RVO at EURETINA 2026
articles.content_orig:
Real-world VOYAGER data at EURETINA 2026 show vision and anatomic outcomes with faricimab across nAMD, DME, and RVO.
New 12-month real-world data from the global VOYAGER study suggest that outcomes with faricimab-svoa (Vabysmo; Genentech) in routine practice are broadly consistent with those reported in its phase 3 trials, with treatment-naive eyes gaining vision and previously treated eyes maintaining or modestly improving vision alongside reductions in retinal thickness and fluid. 1 The findings, which span neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) , diabetic macular edema (DME) , and macular edema following retinal vein occlusion (RVO) , were presented at the 26th EURETINA Congress in Vienna, Austria, held October 1–4, 2026. 1-4
The data are of particular interest to retina specialists because much of faricimab's real-world use involves patients switched from other anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents—a population that was largely excluded from, or underrepresented in, the pivotal trials. 5-7
VOYAGER ( NCT05476926 ) is a prospective, noninterventional study of more than 5,000 patients initiating faricimab 6 mg for nAMD, DME, or RVO across 28 countries in Asia-Pacific, Europe, North America, and South America. 2-4 Treatment followed usual care, with no mandated visit schedule or imaging protocol. 2 Investigators collected visual acuity (VA) in Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) letters, central subfield thickness (CST), investigator-determined subretinal fluid (SRF) and intraretinal fluid (IRF), and ocular safety events. A subset of spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) scans was additionally analyzed using an in-house deep learning segmentation algorithm (ROSA) to quantify fluid volumes in the central 1-mm field. 3,4 All analyses were descriptive. 2-4
“The strength of VOYAGER lies in both its pragmatic design and its broad global inclusion,” Robin A. Vora, MD, a retina specialist at Kaiser Permanente Oakland Medical Center, said in an email interview with the Eye Care Network.
“By omitting protocol-driven appointment and imaging schedules, the study closely mirrors real-world community practice, including high-volume integrated health systems like Kaiser Permanente. Furthermore, by enrolling patients across 28 countries, the dataset aligns well with the diverse patient demographics we care for in Northern California.
As a result, the overall real-world outcomes across all three indications—wet AMD, DME, and RVO—closely resemble what we see in our practice, particularly within the previously treated (switch) population. Where real-world U.S. clinical practice differs from global observational trial data, however, is in the treatment-naïve cohort. In the U.S., insurance coverage preferences and mandated first-line step therapy (such as bevacizumab) often make it difficult for practices to immediately initiate newer generation agents in naïve eyes and, as such, not achieve the rapid early gains reported in VOYAGER.”
In the DME cohort—reported in an abstract by Veeral Sheth, MD, and colleagues—506 treatment-naive and 413 previously treated eyes had at least 12 months of follow-up between November 2022 and January 2026. 2 Among treatment-naive eyes, mean VA improved from 64.1 to 71.1 letters, and mean CST decreased from 415.2 µm to 292.6 µm at month 12. The proportion of eyes with SRF fell from 17.3% to 2.4%, and IRF from 60.8% to 26.8%. 2 In previously treated eyes, VA rose from 66.9 to 69.1 letters and CST decreased from 367.6 µm to 314.2 µm; SRF fell from 10.6% to 4.1% and IRF from 46.3% to 39.1%. 2
Injection frequency declined in the second half of the year, from a mean of 4.3 injections in months 1–6 to 2.1 in months 7–12 in treatment-naive eyes and from 4.1 to 2.7 in previously treated eyes. 2 Per-injection rates of intraocular inflammation (0.05%) and endophthalmitis (0.02%) were low and described by the authors as aligned with the phase 3 program. 2
Genentech's announcement reported somewhat different DME figures, including a mean gain of 8.2 letters and a CST reduction of 127.8 µm in treatment-naive eyes and a 2.7-letter gain in previously treated eyes; the release did not specify the analysis population or explain the difference from the abstract Sheth presented at EURETINA. 1
A separate abstract led by Adrian Koh, MD, applied machine learning segmentation to DME scans from a smaller subset of 28 treatment-naive and 36 previously treated eyes from 14 countries. 3 In treatment-naive eyes, mean total fluid volume decreased from 61.1 nL to 14.3 nL over 12 months, driven by reductions in both SRF and IRF. In previously treated eyes, total fluid fell from 46.7 nL to 26.5 nL, almost entirely through IRF reduction, while SRF volume was minimal and unchanged. 3
In nAMD, the company reported a mean VA gain of 4.6 letters and a CST reduction of 110.5 µm in treatment-naive eyes after 12 months and essentially stable VA (−0.1 letters) with a 26.1-µm CST reduction in previously treated eyes. 1 The proportion of treatment-naive eyes with SRF fell from 72.1% to 25.3%, and with IRF from 48.5% to 20.6%. 1
An imaging abstract led by Clare Bailey, MD, analyzed 136 treatment-naive and 174 previously treated nAMD eyes from 17 countries using the same segmentation approach. 4 Among treatment-naive eyes, mean total fluid volume decreased from 33.1 nL to 3.7 nL and mean pigment epithelial detachment (PED) volume from 43.8 nL to 30.7 nL. In previously treated eyes, which began with lower fluid burden, total fluid decreased from 11.6 nL to 6.4 nL and PED volume from 63.1 nL to 52.7 nL. 4 According to the release, eyes in both the nAMD and DME cohorts received fewer injections in months 7–12 than in months 1–6. 1
RVO results were reported at 6 months and only in the company release. 1 In branch RVO, treatment-naive eyes gained a mean of 10.0 letters with a 171.3-µm CST reduction, while previously treated eyes gained 2.0 letters with a 59.0-µm reduction. In central/hemiretinal RVO, treatment-naive eyes gained 16.6 letters with a 287.4-µm CST reduction, and previously treated eyes gained 3.9 letters with a 63.4-µm reduction. 1 Cohort sizes were not reported.
Faricimab is a bispecific antibody that binds both VEGF-A and angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2); the Ang-2 component is thought to promote vascular stability, although its contribution to clinical response has not been established, according to the prescribing information. 8 The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved faricimab for nAMD and DME in January 2022 as the first bispecific antibody for the eye, followed by approval for macular edema after RVO in October 2023. 8,9
Approval was based on phase 3 trials demonstrating noninferiority to aflibercept 2 mg. In TENAYA and LUCERNE, treatment-naive patients with nAMD gained 5.8 and 6.6 letters, respectively, at the primary end point with dosing up to every 16 weeks. 5,8 In YOSEMITE and RHINE, patients with DME gained approximately 11 to 12 letters at year 1.6,8 In BALATON (branch RVO) and COMINO (central/hemiretinal RVO), mean gains were 16.9 letters in each trial at week 24 with monthly dosing. 7,8 The 72-week extension of those trials evaluated treat-and-extend dosing, and the US label was updated in April 2026 to address RVO treatment beyond 6 months. 8,10
Direct comparison with the trials is limited. Pivotal-trial patients were newly diagnosed and largely treatment naive, whereas VOYAGER includes switched eyes with variable treatment histories and baseline characteristics. The release quoted Robyn Guymer, MBBS, PhD, chair of the VOYAGER steering committee and deputy director of the Centre for Eye Research Australia, who noted that patients in routine practice often do not meet the strict entry criteria of phase 3 trials. 1

articles.title_orig: As measles rages, one clinic leans on years of hard-won trust to keep vulnerable people safe
articles.title_zh: As measles rages, one clinic leans on years of hard-won trust to keep vulnerable people safe
articles.content_orig:
Main Street is bustling on a Wednesday afternoon in late September. Cars mix with horse-and-buggy carriages on the road, many coming and going from the weekly Sale Day — a market spread over 10 acres with livestock, fruits and vegetables, flowers and other goods for available to purchase. Lively conversations in English and Pennsylvania Dutch fill the barn where a produce auction stretches until lunchtime; bids for a pint of bright red cherry tomatoes run from 90 cents to $1.30.
As dozens of people mix and mingle through the afternoon — Amish and other Plain people, so named for their simple way of dressing, as well as “English,” as they refer to folks outside of their community — there are no direct indications that a measles outbreak is raging in the area. Only one woman has a mask on, which she says she’s been wearing any time she’s left home since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic. One vendor is closed for “unexpected family obligations,” and one regular auction attendee is mourned after her recent sudden death after having “flu-like symptoms.” Tourists are visiting from Brooklyn.
But less than a mile away at the Central Pennsylvania Clinic, measles is front and center.
A turn off of Main Street quickly opens up to an idyllic rural valley, filled with lush farms set to a backdrop of rolling green mountains. An unlined road leads across a babbling river to reveal a striking gray building up on a hill, a massive barn raised in the traditional style that uses only wood pegs — no nails — to hold the structure together.
The front door is locked, with a photo and description of measles hanging in the window, along with a notice asking visitors to “ring doorbell for service.” Dr. Katherine Mascia swings the door open with a big smile and a quick question: “Any measles symptoms today?”
Beneath the genuine smile is true heartbreak. A massive measles outbreak in the area — now the deadliest and nearly the largest the United States has had in decades — is bringing significant pain and suffering to the families she cares for.
“In the five years that I’ve worked here, I don’t think we’ve had so many patients admitted to the hospital all within the span of a few weeks,” Mascia said. “We might usually have maybe one patient who’s admitted for their complex care needs, but to have so many all at the same time, it’s really unprecedented.”
About 1,000 measles cases have been reported by the Pennsylvania Department of Health since the outbreak started in April, nearly surpassing the record number recorded in South Carolina during an outbreak that started last year and that became the largest in the US since 1992. The clinic’s home of Mifflin County is one the hardest-hit, near the epicenter in neighboring Lancaster County.
The patients who the Central Pennsylvania Clinic serves are especially vulnerable to the severe effects of a measles infection. The nonprofit is centered around caring for children and adults with genetic disorders that are especially common among the Amish and broader Plain community, a group that also tends to have lower vaccination rates than average.
The Plain people are known for their ​caution toward government and other nonreligious authority.
But as measles tears through many of their hometowns in central Pennsylvania, the national conversation has become paradoxically politically charged.
Leaders from the federal government and the Pennsylvania government have clashed over the response , with much of the debate centered around the five deaths that have come during this outbreak. Disputes over the definition of what counts as a measles death and how news of the deaths is shared with the public have disrupted public health response plans.
Meanwhile, the Central Pennsylvania Clinic’s staff is focused on how to best keep everyone safe and healthy. They’re leaning on the clinic’s well-forged foundation of trust. It has taken persistence and patience — sometimes years — for the clinic to build those relationships, and the strength of that trust has faced some of its greatest tests over the past few months.
When Pennsylvania reported a measles-associated death in an 18-year-old in Mifflin County, Mascia said, the clinic started to get tons of calls — from patients they knew and other members of the broader community — who just wanted to know what happened. They weren’t paying attention to what government officials were arguing about on social media, she said. They wanted a clear understanding of how the young person died.
“I’m quite honored that they’re calling us and asking those questions. It helps me feel like they really trust us,” Mascia said. “But it puts pressure on us, too.”
She said she reached out to the county coroner directly to get a formal statement on the cause of death, and she references that statement when patients have questions.
“We want to keep that line of communication open with the community, and it’s so important to provide accurate information and be consistent with the messaging,” she said.
Central Pennsylvania Clinic leaders have been thinking about and planning for a measles outbreak in the community since the start of the West Texas outbreak in January 2025, Mascia said. Their patients are vulnerable, and their offices, while incredibly well-equipped in many ways, are not built to treat measles patients.
“We don’t have advanced ventilation systems, and we don’t have negative-pressure rooms, so if a person who is infected with measles comes in, our entire building is compromised for two hours,” Mascia said.
Pennsylvania requires a throat swab, a blood sample and a urine sample to confirm a measles case — arduous tasks for both ill patients, who often had to take a taxing horse and buggy ride to the clinic, and for clinic staff who have to work within the constraints of their facility.
The rear entrance to the clinic building, which also hosts a federally qualified health center, has become a makeshift triage center for people with suspected measles cases. The back parking lot is large enough for cars and buggies to spread out, and clinic staffers meet families at the door, where they can lead the patient into a small storage barn to collect urine samples.
It was important to have a logistical plan to keep operations safe, Mascia said, but she pointedly explains that the most critical way to protect their patients is to raise vaccination rates.
The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely effective. One dose is 93% effective against measles, and the recommended second dose bumps that protection up to 97% — and the immunity is lifelong. Extensive research has also demonstrated the vaccine’s safety .
Childhood vaccination rates have been falling nationwide, with a record share of parents opting to exempt their new kindergartners from the required shots last school year.
Vaccination rates tend to be lower among Plain people, but it’s not because of an inherent opposition, experts say.
There are certain shared values within the community, but there are also varied individual beliefs and opinions about vaccines, as there would in any broad group of people, Mascia said. Consistency in the clinic’s messaging around vaccination has been the key to raising coverage rates.
If the patients sense any type of coercion from doctors or if they feel forced into a decision about something like a vaccination, they’ll completely disengage from all health care – an outcome that would be particularly troublesome for the vulnerable patients they care for.
“We share that it’s our strong recommendation that everyone be fully vaccinated,” Mascia said. “And if they’re not interested, we repeat our recommendation and say ‘we’re here to help if and when you change your mind.’”

articles.title_orig: The School Near Paris That Shows Why French Students Are Protesting
articles.title_zh: The School Near Paris That Shows Why French Students Are Protesting
articles.content_orig:
Paris, France – At least 250,000 students, teachers and parents protested across France on Tuesday , supported by trade unions and rights groups.
The demonstrations have grown since students began blockading the entrances to their high schools on September 17, starting in the Paris suburb of Creteil. The movement quickly spread throughout the city’s suburbs, with high schoolers protesting against conditions, lamenting dilapidated buildings, shortages of teachers and staff and overcrowded classrooms.
The blockades were met by a muscular police response, with riot police sent to break up the student protests.
More than 6,000 protesters have been arrested, 85 percent of them aged under 18. At least 10 investigations into police misconduct have been opened by France’s police watchdog IGPN.
On October 2, France’s Education Minister Edouard Geffray met with student leaders and the government announced a five-point plan to reform the public education system – an olive branch students agreed was insufficient to address the crisis.
Some 210 teenagers – including one who lost a hand – and 715 police officers have been wounded, according to officials.
Anne Savinel-Barras, president of Amnesty International France, called on authorities to “avoid unnecessary and excessive use of force”.
“Footage and testimonies widely reported over the last week raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of tear gas, batons and restraint techniques by police. Tear gas grenades have been discharged recklessly, and rubber bullets have been fired causing serious injuries.”
Al Jazeera spoke to several protesters about their demands:
Theo, 19, student : “This is my first demonstration. I’m here in solidarity with the high schoolers, after this week of blockades and police oppression. I’m also here for other demands: for universities, for more resources for schools, and not just schools but hospitals too. We’re really short of resources.
“Macron’s government has to stop investing only in war. We’re fed up. That’s why we’re all here together in this movement of solidarity, young and old. We all have the same demands: a better future.”
Olympe, 16, high school student : “We blockaded our school all week to demand our rights and to denounce what’s happening in our schools. Teachers are absent, and compared with schools in Paris we don’t have the same resources. We’re given less money, and we don’t have the same privileges.”
Rania, 15, high school student: “We don’t feel listened to at all. We feel inferior, especially considering that we’re the future. So when no one listens to us, we do all this, but in the end will it really change anything? We don’t know.”
Maissene, student : “We came to support our classmates, simply because if they’re blockading, we blockade too. It’s a general movement, and they can’t do it on their own.”
Raphael, 17, high school student : “We came to defend our youth. Because we’re young, the state doesn’t listen to us. They think we have no political awareness and don’t know what we’re defending. We’re here to show the opposite: we know exactly what we’re defending. We know our values.”
Rose, 16, high school student: “If nothing changes, we’ll keep going for much longer. On October 17, there will be a big demonstration, with high schoolers, students and farmers. So it’ll be a bit like a new revolution.”
Clemence, 30, maths teacher in Paris : “I support the high schoolers’ movement 100%. Their demands are ones we’ve been making for years. Today, we’re taking the opportunity to march alongside them. They’re asking for more resources, more teachers, better teaching conditions. We’ve been asking for this for years, because the state badly neglects it … You saw how the heatwave was handled: our classrooms were between 35 and 40°C. It’s unacceptable.”
Clara, 20, fashion student: “I’m here first of all in support of the high schoolers who started this strike in the 93 [Seine-Saint-Denis]. It’s where I live, and I know these schools. They have always lived and worked in unacceptable conditions. Their demands are legitimate, and they have a right to be heard and listened to.
“So far I think the atmosphere is rather good. You can see everyone is mobilised, proud and happy to be here. But you can also feel a lot of anger, because for once we want our demands to be heard, and we want people to listen to this youth that has been complaining for several years.”
Tina, a 20-year-old student: “Yesterday we had a general assembly at our university, and the police and riot police were called in by our own administration. We said that was unacceptable. They started blocking our university, blocking our ideals of defending the high schoolers and the current cause. We don’t find that normal, so we came to demonstrate with them today to show our support. In the end there were no classes. We hadn’t finished expressing ourselves. We were peaceful, and they chose violence.”

articles.title_orig: Texas set to execute man for fatally shooting a convenience store clerk in 2000
articles.title_zh: Texas set to execute man for fatally shooting a convenience store clerk in 2000
articles.content_orig:
DALLAS — A Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk is set to die by lethal injection on Wednesday in what would be the nation’s 30th execution this year.
Jamaal Howard, 46, was found guilty of capital murder in the 2000 killing of Vickie Swartout, 42, who was shot once in the chest. He is set to receive a lethal dose of pentobarbital in the first scheduled execution in the U.S. since Tennessee’s failed attempt at putting Christa Pike to death last week.
Pike’s attorneys said Tuesday that she was awake and speaking as she received treatment at a hospital.
Texas has executed six people so far this year, with two more scheduled after Howard.
Swartout was fatally shot during the robbery at the store in the small, rural town of Silsbee, located about 100 miles (161 kilometers) northeast of Houston. Evidence presented at the trial included the store’s surveillance video, which showed Howard shooting Swartout.
Howard, who was 20 at the time, took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store, according to court records.
His attorneys have argued that Howard is intellectually disabled and his execution should be halted. The state said that he has not presented evidence that would show he meets the requirements for a claim of intellectual disability.
He has an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court pending to stop the execution.
The Supreme Court in 2002 had barred the execution of intellectually disabled people. But it has given states some discretion in how they determine such disabilities.
Florida has carried out 16 executions so far this year, the most of any state. Most states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary method.

articles.title_orig: California pair charged with abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children
articles.title_zh: California pair charged with abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children
articles.content_orig:
A California pair has been charged with multiple counts of abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children - some as young as two months old - and dissuading a witness.
"The number of children who were subjected to this alleged horrific abuse is unprecedented," Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan J Hochman said in a statement.
Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang, who US media describe as a couple, were arrested at their Arcadia mansion on Tuesday.
The pair pleaded not guilty at a Pasadena courthouse, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.
Xuan, 66, and Zhang, 39, are accused of conspiring to subject 15 of the 16 children living in their home to repeated physical abuse, after 21 children were removed from their custody last year.
The pair ran their own surrogacy company and are accused of making false statements to at least two women who became surrogates, indicating that Zhang was struggling to conceive, according to the criminal complaint.
As of May 2025, Zhang maintained a spreadsheet that tracked 21 children, including those born to surrogates.
Officials said the investigation began that month when Zhang brought a two-month-old boy to the hospital with a head injury, telling medical staff that the baby had fallen from a bed.
The couple's lawyer Mitchell Krems said the allegation was a "mischaracterisation" based on the evidence he has reviewed, CBS News in Los Angeles reported.
Hospital staff informed law enforcement, and when police arrived at their home they discovered three different rooms called "learning centres" under the supervision of multiple nannies, which Hochman described as a "house of horrors".
The mansion allegedly had 32 motion-activated cameras which Hochman said were used by the couple to monitor the discipline given by the nannies.
Footage allegedly shows the nannies spanking, slapping or hitting the children.
One nanny, Chunmei Li, is accused of hitting the two-month-old baby who suffered the head injury two days before he was brought to the hospital.
Krems said Li was quickly fired, CBS News LA reported.
Li, 58, was previously charged with one felony count of child abuse under conditions likely to cause great bodily injury or death. Hochman said she was on the run with a $105,000 (£88,800) warrant for her arrest.
In July 2025, the couple's home was first raided by authorities, who took 21 children into state custody.
Arcadia Police Department said at the time the couple's house was first raided that the children ranged in age from two months to 13 years old, but most were between one and three years old.
Fifteen of the children were taken from the couple's home while six others were living elsewhere and also later taken into custody.
Krems said his client Xuan was innocent.
"He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family," CBS News quoted the lawyer as saying.
Investigators believe the surrogate mothers were from around the country and they were unaware they were carrying embryos for the couple at the same time.
Melissa Brisman, the attorney for two of the surrogates, told CBS News: "This is wonderful news that people will be held responsible for their actions and there will be consequences if you abuse the surrogacy system".
If convicted as charged, Xuan faces a possible maximum sentence of 17 years and four months in state prison, while Zhang faces up to 11 years and eight months. Li faces up to 12 years.
