articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Isaias forms in the Gulf, set to rapidly intensify into dangerous Cat 2 hurricane by Friday
articles.content_orig:
Tropical Storm Isaias will be the Atlantic's first hurricane in 2026, and the first landfalling hurricane in the U.S. since 2024. FOX Weather Hurricane Specialist offers exclusive insight into the forecast as tropical alerts are issued for the Coastal Gulf.
The first Hurricane and Storm Surge Watches have been issued for the northern Gulf Coast as Tropical Storm Isaias continues to strengthen in the southern Gulf and is forecast to rapidly intensify into a dangerous Category 2 hurricane.
Isaias is expected to approach the coast by Friday, with landfall currently estimated to be sometime late Friday or early Saturday between Biloxi , Mississippi , and Panama City , Florida .
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has declared a state of emergency ahead of the storm.
Isaias strengthened from Tropical Depression Nine in the Bay of Campeche early Wednesday and currently has sustained winds of 45 mph and is moving east-northeast at 8 mph.
HURRICANE RACHEL FORECAST TO TURN BACK TOWARD LAND, BRINGING DANGEROUS SURF TO CALIFORNIA AS SIMON LOOMS
The storm is both compact and moving into a favorable environment for development, which forecasters say will allow it to reach hurricane strength by Thursday.
According to the FOX Forecast Center, Isaias is expected to rapidly intensify with winds going from 40 mph to 75 mph between Wednesday morning and 2 a.m. Thursday. Additionally, winds are expected to ramp up and reach 110 mph between 2 a.m. Thursday and 2 a.m. Friday.
Isaias' forecast cone shows it heading directly toward the northern Gulf Coast, with impacts centered over roughly 30 million people in Louisiana , Alabama , Mississippi and the Florida Panhandle.
LATEST FROM FOX WEATHER HURRICANE SPECIALIST BRYAN NORCROSS
A Storm Surge Watch is now in effect from the Mouth of the Mississippi to Yankeetown, Florida, in the state's Big Bend region.
"The combination of a dangerous storm surge and the tide will cause normally dry areas near the coast to be flooded by rising waters moving inland from the shoreline," the NHC said.
Currently, between 5 and 7 feet of surge is forecast for Mobile Bay and from Ocean Spring, Mississippi, to Indian Pass, Florida.
A Hurricane Watch is in effect from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass, Florida.
Heavy rain is expected to begin on Friday, with flash flooding , damaging wind gusts, storm surge and even tornadoes possible as the storm comes ashore.
There is still some uncertainty regarding exactly where and how strong Isaias will be at landfall.
Florida's State Emergency Response Team is beginning to stage fuel, water and food, according to the governor's emergency declaration.
Today, I signed Executive Order 26-202, declaring a state of emergency for 25 counties in preparation for Tropical Depression Nine. This order ensures communities have the time and resources necessary to prepare for potential severe weather impacts to the Panhandle and Big Bend region of Florida. Floridians should have their plans in place, keep emergency supply kits fully stocked, and follow @FLSERT for weather updates and preparedness information.
Hurricane Hunters are now conducting regular reconnaissance missions into Tropical Storm Isaias, to collect the latest forecast data.
FOX WEATHER JOINS THE HURRICANE HUNTERS ON CRITICAL RECON MISSION INTO TROPICAL STORM ISAIAS
Isaias is forecast to remain in the southern Gulf for much of the day on Thursday, bringing heavy rain to the Yucatán Peninsula, before making a sharp turn towards the northern Gulf Coast as it's grabbed by a strong dip in the jet stream .
FOX Weather Correspondent Brandy Campbell joins the Hurricane Hunters on critical recon mission into Tropical Storm Isaias.
The storm is expected to continue to strengthen and rapidly accelerate early Friday, with heavy rain reaching parts of the Gulf Coast as early as Friday morning.
"Residents from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle should closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure they have their hurricane plan in place," the NHC said.
The NHC also said it is increasingly likely that Isaias will be a significant hurricane when it reaches the coast.
FOX Weather Hurricane Specialist Bryan Norcross noted that several dynamic factors still remain at play, which will determine how strong and exactly where Isaias will make landfall, namely the storm's angle of approach and how the winds will impact the storm as it comes ashore.
TIMELINE: WHERE TROPICAL STORM ISAIAS IS HEADED AND WHEN IT COULD BECOME A HURRICANE
Some forecast models show Isaias weakening at landfall, while others show the storm strengthening as strong winds high in the atmosphere interact with it from the north.
Norcross said most of the storm's most impactful weather will most likely be on the right side of the storm's center.
Meanwhile, NOAA 's Weather Prediction Center (WPC) has issued a flash flood risk for Friday across portions of Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama , Florida, Georgia, as well as southern portions of Tennessee , southwestern North Carolina and western South Carolina .
A Level 3 out of 4 flash flood risk covers Mobile , Alabama, and the Florida Panhandle west of Panama City . A Level 2 risk includes Atlanta and Montgomery , Alabama, and eventually shifts inland into Saturday to include the Carolinas and Tennessee Valley.
"Rainfall estimates currently show 6-10 inches with localized higher amounts which will lead to flash and urban flooding and eventually river flooding," the FOX Forecast Center said.
NOAA's Storm Prediction Center (SPC) has issued a Level 2 out of 5 risk of severe weather for Saturday across southern Alabama and into the Florida Panhandle, with a particular threat of tornadoes as the storm's outer bands come ashore.
Gulf water temperatures are currently at their warmest levels on record dating back to 1982. Warm waters are conducive for tropical development.
September ended without a hurricane for the first time in 32 years, despite it being the climatological peak of the season.

articles.title_zh: Ukraine Claws Back Land in the Donbas, Thwarting a Russian Push
articles.content_orig:
The Russian president, Vladimir V. Putin, has repeatedly said that the fall of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine is inevitable and will happen faster than Kyiv thinks.
Recent trends on the battlefield paint a different picture.
A monthslong Ukrainian counteroffensive in the northern part of the Donbas has thwarted Russian efforts to encircle the remaining Ukrainian-controlled cities in the region. Russia, Western analysts say, has lost dozens of square miles of territory during the Ukrainian campaign, which Kyiv is calling Operation Vivaldi.
In the southern Donbas, Russia continues to mount furious assaults to break through Ukrainian lines. But Kyiv has reorganized its defense there and has so far kept the Russian military from pressing farther in its efforts to surround the major Donbas cities.
More broadly, Russian gains across Ukraine have slowed markedly in 2026 from their already glacial pace of last year. September was the worst month in net territorial gains for Russia inside Ukraine since June 2023, according to the Finland-based research firm Black Bird Group.
While Western researchers who track the battlefield report varying numbers, they generally agree that Russia has gained only slightly more land than it has lost this year.

articles.title_orig: An early flu season means it might be time to think about a flu shot
articles.title_zh: An early flu season means it might be time to think about a flu shot
articles.content_orig:
An early start to the flu season means it might be time to consider a flu shot. Rebecca Blackwell/AP hide caption
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Fall has only just begun, but it's already time to start thinking about the quintessential winter bug: the flu .
The annual flu season usually starts in October or November. But this year, it looks like the flu started to pick up in early September.
"There are enough signs pointing in the same direction to make me think, 'OK, yes. This is the start of flu season,'" says Caitlin Rivers , an epidemiologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
The percentage of people testing positive for the flu in the West has been rising steadily since around the beginning of September, she says. And the number of people showing up in emergency departments because of the flu has also been rising for weeks, she adds.
"It's very uncommon to see flu activity rising this early. It's activity that we might normally see more like November or December," she says.
The timing of the flu season isn't the only thing that's odd. It's also unusual that flu activity seems to have started in Western states, such as California, Washington, Hawaii and Alaska.
"It typically starts in the South and then expands from there," Rivers says. "So two uncommon developments there."
Rivers stresses that the amount of flu activity is still very low in most parts of the country. But that's starting to change as the flu picks up nationwide.
It's unclear why flu activity would have started so early, and in such an unusual part of the country. But one clue might be a new variant that evolved a mutation, which appears to make it better at evading existing immunity, especially among teenagers.
"That's our best argument for what's going on right now in terms of this early flu season," says Dr. Alex Greninger , a virologist who heads infectious disease diagnostics at the University of Washington. Doctors there are seeing as much flu right now as they usually would around Christmas, and the mutated variant appears to be common, he says.
So Greninger, Rivers and others are urging people to think about getting their flu shot earlier than usual.
"It's crucial that people get an influenza vaccine," says Scott Hensley , a virologist at the University of Pennsylvania. "And this might be a year that people might want to get a vaccine early."
But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention hasn't been promoting flu shots as it usually does. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who oversees the CDC, is a long-time vaccine skeptic.
"It is disappointing that CDC is quiet given that flu kills of hundreds of kids a year and can result in tens of thousands of hospitalizations and tens of thousands of deaths," says Dr. Demetre Daskalakis , who resigned last year as the director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to protest what he called political interference at the agency.
The CDC declined to make an official available to NPR for this story. In a statement, a CDC spokesperson said, "CDC is developing a communications strategy to provide clear, accessible information about influenza vaccination and other critical steps people can take to protect themselves during respiratory virus season. This includes information about the benefits and risks of vaccination to support informed decision-making."

articles.title_orig: Other Worlds Than These by Stephen King and Peter Straub review – a self-indulgent finale to the Talisman trilogy
articles.title_zh: Other Worlds Than These by Stephen King and Peter Straub review – a self-indulgent finale to the Talisman trilogy
articles.content_orig:
There are moments of shivering joy as the protagonist of two enduring classics, Jack Sawyer, returns – but this time his journey feels endlessly repetitive
B ear with me, because there is some backstory to get through before we can talk about the book I am actually here to review. Back in 1984, Stephen King and Peter Straub collaborated on the fantasy novel The Talisman. Like all the best King stories, it follows a young boy: in this case Jack Sawyer, 12, whose mother, Lily, is dying. Jack learns that a magical object called the Talisman might save her – if he can find it in a parallel world known as the Territories. Straub and King followed this up in 2001 with Black House , in which an adult Jack investigates a series of child murders that turn out to have disturbing links to the Territories.
The books are very different: one a coming-of-age cross-country quest, in which Jack flips back and forth between two versions of the US; the other a fantastical and horror-inflected murder mystery. Both are brilliant and enduring classics which will always have a place on my bookshelves – I reread both of them, all 1,800-odd pages, to prepare for Other Worlds Than These and was as swept away and delighted as the first time round.
So: in 2013 Straub had an idea for a final volume in the Talisman trilogy, drawing as Black House does from a real-life series of murders, and returning Jack (previously left on a bit of a cliffhanger) to the fray. King didn’t pick up on it back then, and Straub died in 2022 . Now King is 79, and, as he writes in a somewhat valedictory afterword, “it’s time to think about tidying up, as much as such things are possible for a writer whose mind is still crammed with cool ideas”. So he went back to that old idea – the original email lost, but the concept of a “series of motiveless, brutal crimes” in the Far West of the Territories, as Straub put it, at the story’s heart.
Jack, “his tide … going out”, is now 57. An aimless, lonely émigré to the Territories, he is sent on a mission by the two-bit despot he now depressingly reports to. He’s to travel through the toxic Blasted Lands to gather information on the Great Gorge, a mysterious area of “growing danger” that Governor Youngblood wants to know more about. Flipping back and forth between “America-side” and the Territories, Jack learns that an old policeman friend has gone missing on the trail of a pair of “murderin’ kids” who have been leaving a swathe of bodies in their wake in Nebraska. These kids are, he’s told, “infested” by demons – and the infestation is spreading to the children of the Territories.
For the true King fan (the “Constant Reader”, as he puts it), there are moments of shivering joy in Other Worlds Than These – not least in the title, which draws from a key scene in King’s The Gunslinger. I could never not find pleasure in a billy-bumbler (a dog-like creature), or in memories of Wolf, a wonderful creation from The Talisman, or in references to chief gunslinger Roland Deschain from the Dark Tower series. As befits King, there are moments of true horror too, and good ones, as the teenage infection spreads across the Territories.
But I cannot recommend that anyone who is not a Constant Reader embark on this 800-plus-page tome. For one, it would be pointless to read it without previously having read The Talisman and Black House (and if I’m honest, probably the seven-volume Dark Tower sequence too). And even for the Constant Reader, this is really not vintage King. I would have said that I’d follow Jack Sawyer anywhere, but as Ole Travellin’ Jack crisscrossed his way across the dry desert land of the Territories, his journey started to feel endless, and endlessly repetitive. As Jack’s crew are gearing up to cross yet another rickety bridge over yet another gaping chasm, one character even makes this point when they spot it. “Oh God … talk about repetition.” I hear you, fella! Jack himself does it: “Another echo. They’re becoming tiresome,” he says, in a rather too on-the-nose comment about the eerie (not so eerie the nth time they’re mentioned) similarities between the US and the Territories.
Is this deliberate? Yes, undoubtedly: “ka [destiny] is a wheel”, as we’ve been told (more than once); Jack, as Roland did before him, is treading the path laid out for him in an endless cycle. But this time round, it all gets a little portentous, self-referential and self-indulgent – and, dare I say it, boring.
I still think Stephen King is a genius. I still think The Talisman is the perfect coming-of-age dark fantasy novel. So thank you for the endless hours of reading pleasure, Mr King. But unlike its predecessors, Other Worlds Than These will not be going on my reread shelf.

articles.title_orig: World Shipping Council launch digital global Whale Chart with HUB Ocean
articles.title_zh: World Shipping Council launch digital global Whale Chart with HUB Ocean
articles.content_orig:
Kimberly Mathisen (CEO, HUB Ocean) & Joe Kramek (President & CEO, World Shipping Council) - download a high-resolution version of this image.
7 October 2026 – The World Shipping Council (WSC), in partnership with HUB Ocean, today launched a digital version of the WSC Whale Chart, making global information on measures to protect whales from ships even more accessible.
Since its initial launch in 2023, WSC’s Whale Chart was the first global mapping of all known mandatory and voluntary governmental measures designed to reduce harm to whales from vessels. These include speed restrictions, routing measures, areas to be avoided and measures addressing underwater radiated noise.
By partnering with HUB Ocean to produce the digital Whale Chart, these measures are now easier to explore, easier to keep up to date, and can plug directly into digital tools and operational systems.
“Mariners operate across many different jurisdictions, and the measures in place to protect whales vary from country to country and region to region. Bringing this information together digitally and making it available to mariners on the bridges of the ships they are navigating makes it easier to use in voyage planning and helps crews see where changing course or slowing down can make a real difference,” said Joe Kramek, President & CEO of the World Shipping Council.
“The Whale Chart has already become an important reference point for the shipping industry,” said Kimberly Mathisen, CEO of HUB Ocean. “Our hope is that by making this information easier to work with, it becomes part of more decisions, more voyages and ultimately more action to protect whales.”
The Whale Chart and all its underlying datasets are now available through HUB Ocean’s Ocean Data Platform, an open, cloud-based geospatial platform that turns ocean data into insight and action.
Bringing the Whale Chart into that ecosystem means it can be explored alongside other authoritative datasets such as marine protected areas and other ocean intelligence layers, supporting richer insights and decisions for mariners, ship operators, governments and researchers alike.
Alongside the new digital platform, WSC has released the fourth edition of the WSC Whale Chart handbook, providing a quick regional overview of whale protection measures. The digital Whale Chart complements this with more detailed, searchable and most current information for specific voyage areas.
Whales travel across national boundaries and through some of the world’s busiest shipping routes. Where shipping traffic and whale activity overlap, separating ships from whales is the most effective way to reduce the risk of collisions. Where separation is not possible, measures such as speed reductions can help reduce the risk and severity of ship strikes while also limiting underwater noise.
WSC will continue to update the WSC Whale Chart as measures change and new information becomes available.
The digital WSC Whale Chart on the Ocean Data Platform is available here and a preview is available on WSC’s Whales webpage .
About World Shipping Council
The World Shipping Council is the united voice of liner shipping, working with policymakers and industry groups to shape the future growth of a socially responsible, environmentally sustainable, safe, and secure shipping industry. We are a non-profit trade association with offices in Brussels, London, Singapore and Washington, D.C.
80% of everything we buy has come by ship. World Shipping Council members are the international container and vehicle carriers that make global trade possible by offering cost efficient and effective transport for everything from raw materials, food and machinery parts to consumer essentials like medication, clothes and electronics.
Read more at www.worldshipping.org
HUB Ocean is an independent non-profit foundation, dedicated to unlocking the power of data to protect and restore ocean health. The organization has built the performant geospatial and cloud-based Ocean Data Platform, giving scientists, experts, and organizations seamless access to fit-for-purpose ocean data from both public and private sources. Built for interoperability and speed, the platform is designed to connect a federated ocean data ecosystem and accelerate collective action for a sustainable ocean.

articles.title_orig: WHO endorses lifestyle changes over GLP-1 drugs in child obesity fight
articles.title_zh: WHO endorses lifestyle changes over GLP-1 drugs in child obesity fight
articles.content_orig:
The first-ever international guidelines on managing childhood obesity from the World Health Organization (WHO) are raising the profile of GLP-1 treatments for kids and teens — but with strict criteria and a high degree of caution.
The new global guidance, released on Wednesday , recommends a broad range of interventions to manage diet, boost physical activity and change behaviours for the rising number of global youth living with obesity. And in certain cases, for some older children and teenagers, that could also mean medication or bariatric surgery.
The WHO doesn't recommend medical treatment, surgery or weight-loss devices for children up to the age of nine, the organization notes.
For older youth from the age of 10 to 19, medical treatments may be considered only when a supervised lifestyle program hasn't achieved results, the guidance states, while bariatric surgery should only be an option under strict conditions for youth living with severe obesity.
"The foundation of obesity care for children and adolescents is not medicine or surgery, but access to comprehensive support that enables healthy eating, physical activity and sustainable behaviour change," said Dr. Luz María De Regil, the WHO's director of the department of nutrition and food safety.
Cheaper GLP-1s arrive in Canada: Are they safe?
London, Ont.-based pediatric endocrinologist Dr. Marina Ybarra welcomed the organization's cautious acknowledgement of medications as one avenue to tackle obesity.
Here in Canada, two GLP-1s are approved for weight management for youth aged 12 and up, but young patients typically have to pay for the drugs through their parents' insurance or out of pocket, said Ybarra, who works with Western University and leads the London Health Sciences Centre Children's Hospital pediatric weight management clinic.
Obesity Canada launches partnership aimed at improving care in health system
"The news about WHO encouraging GLP-1 as a possible treatment for children living with obesity — I think it's very good news," she said.
"Because maybe that will help us to get funding through the public system in Canada for children living with obesity. That's my biggest hope."
The WHO's new guidance is meant to tackle skyrocketing rates of obesity among global youth.
Roughly 170 million children and teens around the world between the ages of five to 19 were living with obesity in 2024, the WHO noted. Obesity prevalence in this age group has also quadrupled since 1990, rising from two to eight per cent.
The global recommendations echo recent Canadian guidance to manage obesity in children. That long-awaited 2025 update also called for behavioural and psychological support and, in some cases, additional medical or surgical interventions.
How family doctors navigate the rise of weight loss drugs
Can GLP-1s curb more than your desire for food?
But Canadian physicians recommend only using GLP-1s to manage obesity in children after the age of 12, two years above the WHO's cutoff due, and don't stipulate that medical intervention should only be tried after lifestyle changes.
" There is no evidence to support a stepwise approach whereby pharmacologic and surgical interventions should be offered only if behavioural and psychological interventions prove ineffective," reads the guidance published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal.
"Using shared decision-making with families, health care providers should consider all intervention options."
The WHO, in contrast, focused on the "practicality and universality" of diet, physical activity and behavioural changes as the pillars of obesity management, and it stressed the need for "structured long-term follow-up" in cases where patients use medication alongside other lifestyle interventions.
Weight comes back quickly after quitting GLP-1 drugs: study
GLP-1s and other similar medications — known by household brand names like Ozempic, Mounjaro, Rybelsus, Wegovy and Zepbound — have exploded in popularity among adults to treat obesity and diabetes, and for general weight loss, even without a clear medical need .
The drugs work by mimicking the body's glucagon-like peptide-1 hormone, which helps manage appetite, slow digestion and regulate blood sugar.
Ybarra stressed the medications are now an effective tool for many young patients with obesity, helping to both reduce weight and improve quality of life.
1st generic semaglutide injection for weight loss approved: Health Canada
While some children and teens face similar side effects to older patients, including nausea and other gastrointestinal issues, "we didn't see many of the severe complications that were seen in the adult population," Ybarra noted.
Younger and younger patients are also trying this growing class of drugs.
One U.S. study, published in the medical journal Pediatrics in September , revealed a 310-fold increase in GLP-1 prescriptions for children ages eight to 11, shooting up from 0.03 per cent to more than nine per cent between 2019 and 2026 — though overall use in this younger group remains rare.
Should everyone be on GLP-1s? What the science really tells us about cancer prevention and other benefits
Still, the WHO stressed the need for caution regarding GLP-1 use among children and teens, given limited research and the potential for misuse among certain groups, such as athletes or patients with eating disorders.
The WHO's new guidelines note that overall evidence linked to various medication treatments for childhood obesity, including GLP-1s and other drugs such as metformin or sibutramine, was "generally of low quality due to short term follow-up and evaluation, and [due to] the small numbers of studies and participants."
Ybarra agreed there's a lack of long-term data for the use of GLP-1s among youth, given how new these drugs are for younger patients.
"The data we have though, it's very reassuring and helpful — in terms of there's more benefits than risks."
GLP-1s and cancer prevention: What’s known and what isn’t
As for the line in the sand regarding children under 10 avoiding GLP-1s, the WHO's María De Regil stressed in a Tuesday news conference that the agency "recommends prioritizing other interventions in this age group."
"However, it is clear that the research is going in this area," she said. "Some national pediatric associations may recommend it."
Serena Williams’ return to tennis sparks conversation about GLP-1 drugs in sports
Denmark's Novo Nordisk and U.S.-based Eli Lilly are among the drug makers currently trialling pediatric obesity medications for kids as young as six, though María De Regil wouldn’t speculate on how any of those ongoing trials might change the WHO's recommendations.
Major questions still remain about how children should safely use these types of drugs, and for how long, stressed María De Regil.
"We realize that this is a rapidly evolving field," she said.

She's a two-time RNAO Media Award winner for in-depth health reporting in 2020 and 2022, a silver medallist for best editorial newsletter at the 2024 Digital Publishing Awards, and a 2024 Covering Climate Now award winner in the health category. articles.title_orig: Linux Foundation Launches OpenGrid to Build Open, Shared Infrastructure for the World's Electric Grid
articles.title_zh: Linux Foundation Launches OpenGrid to Build Open, Shared Infrastructure for the World's Electric Grid
articles.content_orig:
New open source initiative integrates and builds a data platform and tools to accelerate grid planning and energy infrastructure deployments worldwide
PRAGUE , Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Open Source Summit Europe – The Linux Foundation , the nonprofit organization enabling mass innovation through open source, today announced the launch of OpenGrid, a new initiative building open source infrastructure to modernize power grid planning worldwide. Hosted by the Linux Foundation, OpenGrid creates a neutral, interoperable foundation that allows planners to work across the commercial and open source software they already use, helping reduce the time, cost and technical barriers involved in planning the infrastructure needed to meet rapidly growing electricity demand.
Grid planning has become a critical bottleneck as electricity demand grows, new data center and industrial loads come online and more generation and storage seek connection. More than 2,500 gigawatts of generation, storage and large-load projects are currently pending in grid connection queues worldwide, while annual grid investment needs to roughly double to more than $600 billion by 2030 . Meeting long-term energy needs will require adding or replacing 80 million kilometers of power lines by 2040, yet planning remains constrained by fragmented data, incompatible software and modeling capabilities that are inaccessible to many institutions and countries.
"Open source has repeatedly shown that shared architecture and interoperability accelerate innovation across entire industries," said Jim Zemlin, CEO of the Linux Foundation. "OpenGrid will bring the proven model of open collaboration to grid planning for faster and more reliable deployment. The Linux Foundation's neutral governance will ensure durability, longevity and usability of the technologies that support essential public-interest infrastructure."
OpenGrid is not developing a single replacement for existing grid planning software. Instead, it provides a shared data and interoperability layer that allows existing commercial and open source tools to work together. Its foundational efforts will include open standards and schemas, programmatic APIs and a centralized Data Hub for validated, model-ready datasets. Its first lighthouse application, the OpenGrid Translator, is in development for release in 2027 and will enable data and models to move between widely used commercial platforms and open source tools.
Access to modern planning capabilities is particularly uneven in fast-growing markets. At the same time, emerging economies are expected to account for nearly 80% of global electricity demand growth through 2030 . OpenGrid aims to give planning teams everywhere access to high-quality modeling capabilities, while enabling regulators, advocates and other stakeholders to inspect the models and data informing major infrastructure decisions.
"Reliable electricity supports healthier lives, stronger communities and economic opportunity, but delivering it requires credible plans. Today, too many plans rely on data others cannot verify and tools much of the world cannot afford," said Alice Yake, vice president of BE-GRIDS and chair of the OpenGrid Management Committee. "OpenGrid changes that: open data, open standards and access to planning tools that any utility, regulator or country can inspect and use."
Over time, the OpenGrid ecosystem plans to expand to include open solvers, no-code graphical interfaces, standardized planning workflows and integrations that use AI to support data preparation. By providing transparent, repeatable and accessible planning infrastructure, OpenGrid aims to help planners, infrastructure owners, regulators and communities work from a common technical foundation and make infrastructure decisions with greater confidence faster.
OpenGrid launches with support from Breakthrough Energy GRIDS, Global Grid Catalyst, Connected Grid Initiative and Google.org, with technical delivery partners including Open Energy Transition, Tapestry, TransitionZero and QXT Energy.
Organizations, researchers, regulators and community members interested in contributing to OpenGrid or learning more are encouraged to visit https://www.opengrid.org .
"Electricity systems are going through some pretty radical changes, with many new variable producers, storage and consumers connecting to the grid. OpenGrid supports the infrastructure we need to get quick consensus on how the energy transition should proceed, and to foster the innovation we need to drive it forward faster."
– Tom Brown, Professor of Digital Transformation in Energy Systems, TU Berlin and Managing Director, PyPSA Labs
"Planners shouldn't have to choose between the tools they already use and the open ones now emerging. Building enterprise-grade, open modeling software with Scenario Builder showed us how much time is lost moving data and models between formats. OpenGrid's shared standards and translators tackle that directly, and we're glad to help build them, so that planners anywhere can pick up a model, inspect it, use it and make decisions that cut the time it takes to build clean energy at scale."
– Matt Gray, Co-Founder and CEO, TransitionZero
"Accelerating scientific progress requires turning foundational research and open data into real-world solutions. Power grids are among humanity's most complex engineering systems, yet modeling them is too often limited by fragmented tools and closed data. OpenGrid will provide the shared digital foundation needed to make faster, more evidence-based decisions and ultimately strengthen our global grid infrastructure."
– Joseph Hassine, Scaled Impact Lead, Google.org
"OpenGrid is the catalyst that the power and energy industry needs to drive new software innovations that ultimately will produce better and faster decision making for the power grid. We keep hearing that these times are unprecedented and yet we have seen very few changes in the power software space. OpenGrid's ambitions to demonstrate that open source can be the driver for much needed innovation is something that QXT Energy is enthusiastic to support."
– José Daniel Lara, Co-Founder and CTO, QXT Energy
"The accelerating complexity of the modern power system demands better integration of economic and reliability planning tools, as well as coordinated planning across the transmission and distribution networks. OpenGrid is tackling this ambitious challenge by enabling these diverse tools, whether open source or commercial, to work together and by providing validated datasets. This has the potential to revolutionize grid planning across the globe."
– Debbie Lew, Executive Director, Energy Systems Integration Group (ESIG)
"At OpenET, we make water use data open and accessible, so I've seen firsthand how a shared baseline builds trust among diverse stakeholders. That experience convinces me that open data infrastructure is essential to sound resource management. By giving planners, regulators and communities a common ground truth they can all inspect and understand, OpenGrid will help them make the decisions the energy transition demands."
– Luis Villa, Board Chair, OpenET, Inc.
"Transparent and neutral governance ensures that all interested users have access to the tools in this initiative. It allows users to decide what is best for their purposes, and it keeps the door open for new tool development to foster innovation and avoid lock-in. Transparency in decision-making creates community buy-in. When parties come together on shared infrastructure, working toward common objectives and the methods and results can be vetted by many parties, this builds the trust and sense of fairness and legitimacy that will be necessary for OpenGrid to be successful."
– Karin Wadsack, Executive Director, Global Power System Transformation Consortium

MINNEAPOLIS – General Mills has been named one of the World’s Best Employers 2026 by Forbes. This prestigious award recognizes organizations setting the gold standard for workplace excellence and is presented by Forbes and Statista Inc., the world-leading statistics portal and industry ranking provider.
General Mills’ results were driven by the company’s work to invest in employees’ development, well-being and a culture where belonging is a daily reality, not simply a stated value.
“At General Mills, our people are at the heart of our success,” said Jacqueline Williams-Roll, Chief Human Resources Officer at General Mills. “We invest in their growth and development, take a whole-person approach to well-being, and work every day to build a culture where everyone feels they belong and can do their best work. Our ambition is to be the best place to grow a career, and we’re proud of our progress.”
The World’s Best Employers were selected based on an independent survey of more than 300,000 employees across 50 countries working for multinational companies with at least 1,000 workers. The final list recognizes the top 900 companies globally. articles.title_orig: Why AI is both the hope and the hazard for world leaders, according to IMF chief Georgieva
articles.title_zh: Why AI is both the hope and the hazard for world leaders, according to IMF chief Georgieva
articles.content_orig:
SINGAPORE — The technology that investors and governments are counting on to lift the global economy is also adding pressure that threatens growth, the head of the International Monetary Fund said, urging policymakers to stop delaying painful choices on debt.
Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told the audience at a Wednesday event in Singapore that artificial intelligence is "rapidly becoming a key driver of countries' relative fortunes in the world economy."
But the triple forces of AI advancement, soaring energy costs and record public debt are challenging the already "underwhelming" growth this decade.
"Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here," Georgieva said.
Speaking ahead of a series of IMF and World Bank annual meetings that kick off next week, Georgieva framed the global economy as being tugged in two directions at once: a "negative energy supply shock" from the war in the Gulf, now in its eighth month, and a "positive demand shock" from the AI investment boom. The combined effect, she said, is "highly uneven across the world."
On the upside, global AI investment as a share of GDP will reach, and likely exceed, the amounts that went into building the railroads, electricity grid, or telecommunications network. AI hardware and related technology products already account for more than a tenth of world goods trade, she said.
The IMF estimates that AI could add up to half a percentage point to annual world growth if done right. "Going from 3% to 3.5% over a decade — that is like adding an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy," Georgieva said.
But the benefits are likely highly concentrated. The boom largely bypasses economies less involved in the global AI supply chain, "increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe," she said.
The boom also feeds the inflation worry that has dogged policymakers from the U.S. to Europe and Asia. "The AI building boom is inflationary," she said, as are energy and food shocks, tariffs and defense spending.
Oil prices have stayed above $100 per barrel as the Middle East conflict dragged on with few signs of a diplomatic off-ramp. Retail diesel prices also rose to record highs as refining capacity squeezed energy supplies.
That inflation pressure flows straight into bond markets, as bond yields in the U.S., Germany, and Japan have surged to their highest levels in decades . Ballooning long-term private bond issuance by AI-related borrowers also competes with governments for capital, although part of the rise may reflect expectations of faster growth, Georgieva said.
Global public debt is near its highest level since World War II and on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP, with advanced economies the "worst offenders," Georgieva said. For 17 years, governments had "a relatively easy ride" because interest rates stayed below growth rates. "Higher interest rates now put an end to that."
The interest-to-growth differential is now "much less favourable" and "set to climb higher," she said, which means the growth needed to reduce debt ratios without fiscal effort is now "out of reach in the near term."
The strain is already visible in Europe, where spreads over German bunds are widening not just for France and Italy but for Ireland, Portugal and others that had reduced debt and deficits after the euro-area crisis.
After a string of shocks that have ballooned public debt and most countries' fiscal deficits remained above pre-pandemic averages, "fiscal space is crying out for replenishment," Georgieva said.
Georgieva also pointed to a financial stability risk in the AI boom itself. Strong corporate earnings are driving share prices and wealth effects, she said, but "should earnings fall short, however, hyperscaler leverage and large and growing global holdings of U.S. equities could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock."
Citing Amara's Law, which holds that people overestimate a new technology in the short run and underestimate it in the long run, she said it is "somewhere in the transition between today's AI building boom and tomorrow's arrival of AI's benefits that we will traverse the period of maximum risk."
Georgieva said the first line of defense is regulation and supervision. "Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries' monetary policy," she said.

articles.title_zh: IceCube, high-energy neutrinos, and Francis Halzen win 2026’s Physics Nobel
articles.content_orig:
Credit : Bryce Richter / UW–Madison
An astrophysics column on big questions and our universe.
There’s a whole entire Universe out there, and the more we learn about it as it actually is, the greater our potential becomes to achieve great things as a civilization, even if the path from knowledge to improving humanity is far from clear. The Nobel Prize was set up more than 100 years ago with the express purpose of rewarding those whose work provides the “greatest benefit to humankind” in a number of disciplines, including physics. We couldn’t foresee that:
Similarly, we cannot know what advances will arise in the future from advances made today in fields like elementary particle physics, gravitational waves, or neutrino astronomy, but possibilities range from computational advances to superior timekeeping technologies to extraterrestrial communication. One thing is certain, however: we have to make the fundamental advance, first, if we ever hope to find out. In many ways, that’s what the science of physics is all about.
It’s for that reason that the world ought to be incredibly excited that the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics has gone to Francis Halzen , for “decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” which is a remarkable testament to what a single individual can accomplish with a creative idea, a lot of hard work and organization, persistence, a strong national investment in science, and quite a bit of good luck. Here’s the story of this remarkable advance in neutrino physics and astrophysics.
The idea of IceCube was born 39 years ago, back before “neutrino astrophysics” was a field that went beyond our Solar System. Prior to 1987, neutrino astrophysics was restricted solely to measuring the neutrinos coming from within the Solar System: by building a large tank of fluid deep underground. Starting in 1968 , the idea was that neutrinos from the Sun, occasionally, would interact with an atomic nucleus, transmuting a neutron into a proton, and converting the neutrino into an electron in the process. By looking for the newly transmuted nuclei, solar neutrinos could then be detected.
In principle, nuclear reactions would occur all across the Universe, releasing neutrinos when they did, but the flux would be far too low to detect them. However, due to contemporaneous interest in grand unified theories , particle physicists had begun building much larger tanks of fluid surrounded by photomultiplier tubes, with the idea being to detect any spontaneously decaying protons by measuring their faster-than-light in the liquid medium radiation: Cherenkov radiation .
The major experiment of the 1980s, Kamiokande , was originally an experiment to search for nucleon decay in Kamioka, Japan. Running for several years, it only obtained null results, until the day of February 24, 1987. All of a sudden, an array of signals emerged: 12 of them (antineutrinos, technically) in the Kamiokande II detector alone . Four hours later, the light arrived as well, confirming this was indeed a supernova event. Kamiokande, the Kamioka nucleon decay experiment, kept the same acronym, but renamed itself to the Kamioka neutrino detector experiment. From a failed search for proton decay , the science of neutrino astronomy was born.
Over the subsequent years and decades, most approaches to neutrino detection simply scaled up this approach. Large, underground, liquid-filled detectors lined with photomultiplier tubes optimized to detect Cherenkov radiation were the key to building neutrino detectors, including Super-Kamiokande and the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (SNOLab), where the original research led to a Nobel Prize awarded in 2002 for neutrino physics and the upgraded research led to one in 2015 for neutrino oscillations.
However, in the aftermath of the 1987 supernova and subsequent neutrino detection, Francis Halzen began thinking about a different approach. Giant tanks were fundamentally limited in a key way: the effective volume available for interactions with neutrinos was constrained to be no larger than the size of your tank. If you wanted to find rare events, your only options were to either build a larger tank or to wait for longer periods of time, until such a neutrino from a rare event happened to interact within your detector.
Halzen came up with an alternative in 1988, which he merely (and humbly) referred to as a “cute idea,” which was to do away with a photomultiplier tube-lined tank entirely. Instead, he wondered, given that there’s so much ice located at the Earth’s south pole, could one simply use Antarctic ice as the “detector” for interacting with neutrinos instead?
Of course, it wouldn’t be possible or practical to use the entire Antarctic ice sheet, but Halzen realized that if you restricted yourself to a mere section of it — a large, cubical block — you could vastly increase the potential interaction volume over what you could ever hope to build with a conventional, liquid-filled and photomultiplier tube-lined detector. If it could be implemented successfully, Halzen’s vision could bring about a neutrino detector that was able to see events that were far rarer than the other neutrino detector designs would be sensitive to.
We had a longstanding hint of this from cosmic rays: non-neutrino particles (mostly protons, but also some heavier nuclei) that struck and interacted with Earth’s upper atmosphere, producing energetic particle showers. Sometimes, the daughter particles emerging from the shower could be detected directly on the ground, but most frequently, the shower of particles would interact with the Earth’s atmosphere: moving faster-than-light in the medium of air, and producing a cone of blue light that was once again the hallmark of Cherenkov radiation. Arrays of Cherenkov telescopes routinely detect this light, and reconstruct the signatures (and energies) of the particles that originally created them. When they do, they find that there are cosmic particles out there far, far more energetic than anything we could ever hope to realistically produce in laboratory experiments here on Earth.
If these high-energy particles — albeit, rare particles — are out there in the Universe, ostensibly created by high-energy sources like neutron stars, black holes, and active quasars, then it stands to reason that similar processes will create ultra-energetic neutrinos as well. However, since the number of particles above a given energy rapidly decreases as a function of energy, it would also imply that ultra high-energy neutrino events should be exceedingly rare as well, requiring enormous volumes of “detector material” in order to even see one or a few of them.
Super-Kamiokande is the world’s largest operational neutrino detector tank, holding just over 50,000 tonnes of extraordinarily pure water, but is only about 40 meters on a side. (Technically, in a cylindrical shape.) For comparison, however, if you went deep into the Antarctic ice, you should be able to find ice that is:
Halzen’s idea was to use hot water to bore cylindrical holes straight down into the Antarctic ice at regularly spaced intervals, and then to place specialized Cherenkov detectors down deep within the ice itself, filling the gaps back up with water to restore the ice back to its pristine, block-like state. If these detectors were spaced out over a volume of ice that was a cubic kilometer in size — 1 km × 1 km × 1 km — it would possess 20,000 times the detection volume of Super-Kamiokande!
The prototype for what would become the IceCube neutrino detector was known as AMANDA: the Antarctic Muon And Neutrino Detector Array . AMANDA was made up of optical modules — each with one photomultiplier tube inside to be sensitive to Cherenkov light — that were sunk into the Antarctic ice beneath the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. The rush to develop artificial intelligence is delivering a growth spurt that's so far confined to a handful of countries, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Wednesday in prepared remarks in Singapore ahead of the annual IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok next week.
Meantime the squeeze on key commodity supplies due to conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine is set to continue into 2027, and soaring bond yields have left governments that amassed too much debt under mounting budget pressure, Georgieva said — calling advanced economies the "worst offenders" on the latter count.
"The AI building boom is inflationary. The energy and food shocks are inflationary. Tariffs, defense spending, and high public debt can be inflationary," Georgieva said. She called for a "prudently hawkish bias" on the part of central banks, and said countries that have gotten used to running large budget deficits are in for "some very tough political choices."
The weeklong Bangkok gathering of top finance ministers and central bank governors takes place against a backdrop of turbulence in sovereign debt markets, as yields on US, European and Japanese bonds hit multi-decade highs. Total global debt has now surpassed $365 trillion, according to the Institute of International Finance.
"Policymakers had a relatively easy ride over the last 17 years as for all that time interest rates were stuck below GDP growth rates," Georgieva said. "Higher interest rates now put an end to that."
By contrast, the wave of AI investment — and expectations for the economic gains it will deliver — keeps propeling stocks to new highs, and has delivered record exports for Asia's powerhouse producers of chips and other equipment.
The bond selloff got underway after the US and Israel attacked Iran in February, choking off fuel supplies and raising costs worldwide. Georgieva said the energy shock has been "large but contained" so far. But she warned that "price pressures may build further as demand rises with the approach of the Northern hemisphere cold season and as countries replenish reserves."
The AI buildout is adding to energy demand, and it also risks widening economic inequalities, Georgieva said. "Growth in AI-related trade reflects the investment boom in economies embedded in its value chain," she said, but "it largely bypasses most others."

articles.title_zh: Neat tricks to help French bonds
articles.content_orig:
France’s unprecedented wave of student protests has laid bare the country’s growing financial pressures, which will only become more difficult to tackle as Europe’s second-largest economy tries to rein in a ballooning budget deficit.
The country’s finances are in a precarious state. Public debt was more than $4 trillion in June, exceeding the size of the economy, according to the country’s statistics agency . The cost of servicing that debt has climbed by billions of dollars on last year, as bond yields spike .
At the same time, demands on the public purse are rising: Pension costs have climbed because of an aging population while the government looks to spend more on defense.
High school students, meanwhile, have called for a fix to staff shortages, overcrowded classrooms and crumbling school infrastructure.
Solutions to France’s financial troubles have led to social unrest in the past. Efforts to raise the retirement age sparked widespread protests in 2023 .
French school protests grow as workers join students
Last week, the French government proposed deep spending cuts and tax hikes aimed at narrowing the budget deficit, but bond buyers are concerned that fiscal measures may be watered down by lawmakers ahead of presidential elections next year, said Andrew Kenningham, chief European economist at consultancy Capital Economics.
The election could see President Emmanuel Macron ousted by either a far-right or far-left successor, raising questions over the country’s commitment to fiscal discipline. While Marine Le Pen’s right-wing National Rally recently proposed substantial spending cuts meant to stabilize the public finances, her party also remains committed to costly tax reductions, Kenningham said.
“Investors will also be concerned about greater fiscal populism after the elections,” he wrote in a note last week. “There is a big risk that spreads rise a lot further, either before or after next year’s elections.”
Worries about a potential debt crisis in France boiled over last week, leading to a selloff in French bonds and a sharp rise in yields.
The spread between French and German bond yields expanded to its widest level since 2012. That difference in yields means investors are demanding much higher returns to hold debt from France compared with Germany, which is deemed a safer alternative.
The French bond rout has sparked fears of spillovers to other high-yield European debt markets, with some analysts drawing parallels with the eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s .
Global bond sell-off deepens, sending borrowing costs higher around the world
Given France’s size and systemic importance, “the potential for contagion into other countries and the Eurozone at large is very large and could potentially cause a serious crisis for the entire region,” Angel Talavera, chief European economist at Oxford Economics, an advisory firm, told CNN.
These worries in large part pushed the euro to its weakest level against the dollar since May 2025 on Monday. The currency, shared by 21 countries in the European Union, is worth around $1.12, having briefly dipped below that level.
The latest ructions in markets could weigh on a fragile economic recovery in Europe, bolstered by investment into artificial intelligence, stronger demand for European exports and higher defense spending in Germany.
Recent survey data showed that activity in manufacturing and services in the euro area increased at its fastest pace in nearly three-and-a-half years last month.
“(Economic) growth is staging a comeback and Europe has shown surprising resilience,” economists at Morgan Stanley wrote in a late September note.
Fall of yet another premier will make it hard for France to fix its finances. What’s behind its debt problem?
High bond yields are a clear risk to that growth, however.
If governments don’t cut spending , “interest rates will continue to go up,” Carsten Brzeski, head of macroeconomics at Dutch bank ING told CNN.
Higher bond yields push up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy, making home and car purchases more expensive and driving down investment. They also make it more expensive for governments to borrow money and force a certain degree of austerity to stop yields from rising further.
Yields on French, German and UK government bonds have broken multi-year records in recent weeks as concerns mount about the sustainability of public debt loads.
Europe’s public finances pose “serious risks to eurozone financial markets and to the economy,” Jack Allen-Reynolds, deputy chief eurozone economist at Capital Economics, told CNN.

articles.title_orig: The world’s oyster reefs could add $12 trillion to planetary health each year – if they were better managed
articles.title_zh: The world’s oyster reefs could add $12 trillion to planetary health each year – if they were better managed
articles.content_orig:
Scientists calculated the total gross ecosystem product that the world’s oyster reefs could deliver to planetary health and human wellbeing, given adequate interventions for habitat restoration and protection. They estimated that the combined potential ecosystem services of oyster reefs, including food production, carbon sequestration, water filtration, and coastline protection, could be worth up to $12 trillion per year. For this potential to be realized, 90% of sites suitable for oyster reefs would require restoration, while 80% would need protection through conservation efforts.
A new study shows that the world’s oyster reefs are a precious resource that’s vastly underestimated and underutilized. The authors set out to calculate the reefs’ potential gross ecosystem product (GEP), the ecological counterpart of the gross economic product, and arrived at trillions of dollars of ecosystem goods and services delivered each year to different aspects of planetary health, including human wellbeing. But for their full potential to be realized, oyster reefs around the world will need to be restored and protected.
“Here we estimate that fully restored oyster reefs in the top ten hotspot countries worldwide would yield a GEP of $12 trillion,” said Dr Matteo Convertino, an associate professor at Tsinghua University and the corresponding author of the publication in Frontiers in Marine Science .
The UN’s Sustainable Development Goal ‘Life below water’ calls for the conservation and sustainable use of coastal and marine resources to safeguard human wellbeing. But today, oyster reefs — like all coastal ecosystems — are under growing pressure from overexploitation, pollution, and climate change. Worldwide, an estimated 85% of such reefs have been lost over the past century, especially in estuaries and river deltas.
Convertino and colleagues began by assessing where suitable habitats for oyster reefs exist around the world today and where reefs could spontaneously form, given the right protection and interventions for restoration. They then estimated the potential value of the entire ‘portfolio’ of ecosystem services these reefs could deliver. Besides oysters for human consumption, these include water filtration, shoreline protection, the recycling of nutrients through the food web, and carbon sequestration. Oyster reefs also provide food, shelter, and nursery grounds for a plethora of fish and invertebrates.
Read and download the original article
The scientists imported thousands of geotagged records of oyster reefs from two public databases. They then used a tried-and-tested machine learning algorithm to predict geographic distributions and habitat suitability around the world, and identify potential new locations for reefs. Their estimate of suitability weighed a slew of environmental measures such as local water temperature, salinity, light, nutrient-richness, and oxygenation. Any location with a habitat suitability score of 65% or greater was classified as suitable. By combining a given area’s score with a measure of the ecosystem services that a reef there could provide, the authors rated the ‘ecopotential’ of each location. The higher the ecopotential, the greater the potential benefit.
The results showed that the predicted ecopotential is greatest in ten ‘hotspot nations’: the US, Australia, Chile, China, Japan, South Korea, Argentina, France, Germany, and Italy. Across these countries, approximately 295,000 square kilometers, or 6% of their coastal zones, were deemed to be suitable. Oyster reefs are currently known to occupy only 10% of this area, mainly in lagoons and bays, estuaries, and river deltas: this indicates that there is a lot of room for expansion. Importantly, only 23% of the suitable area is currently under any form of marine protection.
If the entire area with positive ecopotential were occupied by reefs, the authors’ calculations show that these could filter prodigious volumes of water: 77.58 quadrillion liters in the US, 69.92 quadrillion liters in Australia, and 46.58 quadrillion liters in Chile. These reefs could also sequester as much as 12.3 million metric tons of carbon a year. In the US alone, the combined potential value of nitrogen removal, carbon sequestration, and water purification by oyster reefs was estimated at $25.1 billion a year.
However, the authors stressed that these are estimates, which infer ecosystem services from global averages of key parameters, and which could be affected by changes in oyster populations over time or by the climate crisis. Significant work on habitat restoration and protection would also be needed to unlock reefs’ potential.
“We estimated that 90% of sites suitable for oyster reefs require restoration, while 80% need protection through conservation efforts. In other words, the current oyster situation is very suboptimal but there is a huge opportunity, considering the benefits,” said Convertino.
“Because global warming generally decreases the habitat quality of oyster reefs, we expect that their global GEP will go down from the current potential value of $12 trillion. But some countries may see an expansion of reefs due to more favorable conditions for the growth and dispersal of oysters: in particular this could happen in Australia, Indonesia, South Korea, Japan, and France.”

articles.title_orig: Takeaways from the Maine Senate debate between Susan Collins, Troy Jackson
articles.title_zh: Takeaways from the Maine Senate debate between Susan Collins, Troy Jackson
articles.content_orig:
Republican challenged by Democrat Troy Jackson in critical Senate race says she opposes Iran war and Canada tariffs
Susan Collins, the Republican senator for Maine , pointedly distanced herself from Donald Trump in a televised debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, as she sought to present an image of independence in a state that has voted against Trump three times.
Proclaiming herself as not the US president’s “favorite senator”, Collins made the highly unusual boast for a Republican that she had voted with Joe Biden, a Democrat, more than 90% of the time when he was president. She also emphasized her differences with her fellow Republicans , saying she voted against her own party more than any other senator.
Collins’s defensiveness came amid a determined onslaught from Jackson, 58, a veteran former state legislator who was getting his first chance to present himself to a broad audience since replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic candidate in a contest that could be vital to the party’s hopes of winning the Senate.
Platner, a former harbor master, was forced to withdraw from the race in July after facing sexual assault allegations, which he denied, leaving Democrats racing against the clock to replace a candidate who had built up momentum campaigning on a populist progressive platform.
Jackson painted Collins as a Trump loyalist, saying she voted with the president 96% of the time. He also doggedly focused on her 2018 vote for the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, tying it to the court’s subsequent overturning of Roe v Wade, which had for half a century guaranteed the national right to abortion.
“Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in a pithy opening statement. “Eight years ago today, Maine women went to DC and begged Senator Collins not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, but she did it anyways.
“He helped overturn Roe v Wade, and today she says she has no regrets. Would you trust her to pick the next supreme court justice?”
Collins, 73, who has been a senator since 1996, has frequently presented herself as a moderate who stands against more radical trends in her own party. The posture is in line with Maine’s profile as a more Democratic-leaning state, which Trump has not won in any of his three presidential campaigns and which has voted for Democratic presidential candidates in every election since 1992.
Nevertheless, Collins went to unusual lengths to differentiate herself from Trump on a range of issues, including the war with Iran, which she said she voted to end nine times, calling it “not well thought out”.
Collins reacted with something close to alarm when the moderator, Gregg Lagerquist, said Trump had suggested that the president might pay a campaign visit to Maine.

“I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” she said. “He’s talking about going to a lot of different states. I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite senator.”
Collins stressed her differences with the president on specific issues pertinent to the Maine economy, including rural healthcare and tariffs against Canada, with which the state shares a border.
“I have been the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada,” she said. “Canada is not China. It’s our neighbor and our friends.”
Polls show the two candidates running neck and neck.

articles.title_orig: Doja Cat’s ‘Tour Ma Vie World Tour’ tests her performer bona fides
articles.title_zh: Doja Cat’s ‘Tour Ma Vie World Tour’ tests her performer bona fides
articles.content_orig:
When an artist abandons the standard fanfare and extravagance of an arena tour, their true performance ability is put to the test. Doja Cat’s “Tour Ma Vie World Tour” demonstrated her showmanship needs no hefty entourage of backup dancers, elaborate sets or choreography.
The tour, which hit Chicago’s United Center on Oct. 3, traverses the R&B artist’s ’80s-infused 2025 album “Vie,” while incorporating older hits like “Need to Know” and “Say So.” Apart from a handful of male backup dancers and occasional pyrotechnics, her tour is largely an understated affair as she commands the audience’s attention almost entirely on her own.
Opening with a hearty brass interlude, Doja Cat began the evening with “Cards,” the first track on “Vie.” Her performance evoked sartorial themes of the ’80s, as she donned pink geometric yoga pants and a bright orange cheetah-patterned coat. Vibrant lighting punctuated the disco-heavy setlist as Doja Cat ventured further into the album, which combines dance-pop and disco.
Her newest album and its accompanying tour are quite a departure for Doja Cat, whose earlier discography is primarily contemporary R&B and rap.
While the show’s runtime focused heavily on “Vie,” Doja Cat gained substantial mileage from older hits like “Need to Know” from her 2021 album “Planet Her” and “Streets” from her 2019 album “Hot Pink,” a testament to her artistic depth.
The concert presents Doja Cat at her most comfortable, highlighting the signature unseriousness that makes her such a compelling performer. At one point, she playfully lit a cigarette before jumping back into song. Later on, she pied an audience member in the face during a tongue-in-cheek interactive skit.
Though there were scattered moments of grandeur, Doja Cat was at her best when she was alone onstage, commanding the audience without flashy costume changes or theatrical gimmicks.
The most memorable track from the evening was unequivocally “Paint The Town Red,” a hit from her 2023 album “Scarlet.” Unaccompanied by background vocals, Doja Cat exerted a larger-than-life stage presence throughout the track, eliciting deafening cheers from the audience.
True to form, Doja Cat concluded the concert on a high note, launching a pyrotechnics show to close out the night and putting her band centerstage for an epic guitar solo. Bouncing between fan favorites like “Tia Tamera” and new songs like “Stranger,” the artist underscored her thematic versatility as a performer.
Though her performance was notably unostentatious, Doja Cat’s “Tour Ma Vie World Tour” proves she is a born performer. With a refined yet metamorphic style, Doja Cat demonstrated she can be as dynamic as she is iconic.

Jaguar has unveiled Type 01, the most technologically advanced and powerful Jaguar in the brand’s history.
New York, USA, 6 October 2026: Jaguar has unveiled Type 01, the most technologically advanced and powerful Jaguar in the brand’s history. A luxury four‑door GT that never arrives unnoticed.
Type 01 inspired a celebration of contemporary culture across New York. This was a one‑of‑a‑kind premiere, from large‑scale digital displays in Times Square, DUMBO and the Lower East Side, to its dynamic arrival for an exclusive gathering at STORIED in West Chelsea, zip code 10001.
Type 01 is defined by exuberant proportions, with its low roofline, long bonnet, sleek silhouette and dramatic presence. Starting from a single line and a blank sheet of paper, it is the most aerodynamic and powerful Jaguar road car. A bold, one‑of‑a‑kind that breaks convention, with a clear lineage to the great Jaguars of the past including the E‑type and XJS.
Beneath Type 01’s clean surfaces is a bespoke Jaguar Electric Architecture which offers more than 1,000PS, always with power in reserve, for a drive that is unmistakably Jaguar. Powered by an 850‑volt electrical architecture, it delivers a 400‑mile range (EPA) and adds 200 miles in 13 minutes using 350kW charging. Type 01 represents a new standard of power, aerodynamics and technological advancement for Jaguar.
From its dramatic design to its captivating drive, Type 01 distils the essence of Jaguar into a luxury grand tourer for a new era. Type 01 is the foundation of this British brand, one that makes no compromise between design and engineering in our quest to create objects of desire, just as it was in the days of the E‑type and XJS.
At the world premiere of Type 01 at STORIED in New York, Jaguar announced acclaimed actor Florence Pugh as the inaugural brand ambassador for its new era. Embodying the originality, fearlessness and creative spirit that define Jaguar.
Pugh joined guests and friends of the brand to celebrate the global arrival of Type 01 with a night dedicated to bold creativity and artistic expression. British singer‑songwriter Sienna Spiro, Best New Artist at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards, performed an intimate set. Celebrated chef Roze Traoré conceived an exclusive culinary programme inspired by Jaguar's fearless creative vision.
New York provided the brand with an international stage from which to celebrate originality and British innovation – a city where art, fashion, film, music and design create one of the world’s most influential centres of reinvention.
At STORIED NYC, guests encountered a series of product artefacts exploring the artistry that brought the Type 01 vision to life:
The STORIED reveal sequence began with Type 01’s dynamic arrival, driven by António Félix da Costa from the World Championship‑winning Jaguar TCS Racing team.
This was the biggest moment since the Jaguar name was born in 1935. A fitting tribute and a powerful expression of Jaguar's dramatic new era. A new chapter for the brand begins with Type 01. Jaguar is back. Orders open early 2027 with first client deliveries expected in the second half of the year. Prices start from 130,000 GBP.

By Charity L. Cohen / 10/06/2026 Alumni , College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences
EAST GREENSBORO, N.C. (Oct. 6, 2026) – Forever a North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University Aggie and now a Hillman College Falcon, former Mister A&T Joshua Suiter ‘22 is starring in the Netflix reboot of the 1980s and 1990s hit sitcom “A Different World.”
The series, which debuted at No. 1 on Netflix in the U.S., has already been renewed for a second season. It builds on the cultural impact of the original series, which helped shape national perceptions of historically Black college and university (HBCU) life and inspired generations of students.
Following a new generation of students at the iconic fictional HBCU, Hillman College, the sequel explores the lives of today’s students while examining the legacy of those who came before them. The series’ writing team includes Ashley Laverne Jackson, daughter of late civil rights leader the Rev. Jesse Jackson ‘64.
Suiter portrays Andre, a fellow Hillman student alongside Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), daughter of original characters Whitley (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne (Kadeem Hardison). As Deborah begins her journey at Hillman, she works to establish her own identity beyond her parents’ legacy while experiencing the highs and challenges of campus life.
“Seeing all the love for Andre really hit home,” Suiter said. “He’s one of my favorite characters thus far, and we created him from scratch, so to know that the hard work is being received and folks want more encourages me to keep going.”
Suiter discovered his calling for acting and musical theater at 7, quickly realizing that hours spent studying lines and practicing techniques felt like minutes. That passion led him to N.C. A&T, where he earned a B.F.A. in professional theatre from the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences.
While at A&T, Suiter built a strong foundation in the performing arts, gaining experience both on stage and behind the scenes. One of his notable performances was in “Ain’t Misbehavin’” during the university’s first Town & Gown Gala in 2019, where he first met Guy, who reprises her role as Whitley in the reboot.
In addition to acting, Suiter worked as a theater technician and developed skills in the marketing and business aspects of performance and the entertainment industry. This versatility helped propel him into his professional career.
“I came in as a creative, but what A&T did between Alpha Phi Alpha, the classes, talking business with professors and serving as Mister A&T sharpened me on the business side,” said Suiter. “It sharpened my networking skills while showing me how to be authentic to who I am.”
As a talented and emerging actor who most recently appeared in the Hulu series “All’s Fair,” performing alongside prominent Hollywood actors, starring in “A Different World” represents a full-circle moment for Suiter as an HBCU alumnus, bringing him into a reimagined version of a series he grew up watching.
“When you talk about an HBCU experience, I’m putting mine up there with the best of them,” he said. “I have so many experiences to pull from with the run of this show, with the character Andre. Hillman even has a heartbeat of its own, so it’s been fun exploring what that feels like as a student there, while still carrying that Aggie Pride in my heart.”
